## 3. MP launch crash (frame pacing's hardcoded dvar-lookup address)

**Status: Resolved, live-confirmed (2026-09-23).** Direct user report: "mp doesnt even start with the mod installed now." Deterministic, 100%-reproducible crash inside genuinely native `iw5mp.exe` code (confirmed via two independent WER crash dumps, `iw5mp.exe.17464.dmp`/`iw5mp.exe.21816.dmp`, byte-for-byte identical register state and RIP across separate process launches), reached during/around real `IDirect3DDevice9::CreateDevice` -- the log stopped right after `MH_EnableHook(CreateDevice)`, never reaching `Hook_CreateDevice`'s own first log line.

**Investigation dead ends, real but ultimately not the cause (recorded so a future session doesn't retread them):** `FlushLogOnCrash`'s vectored exception handler (confirmed a provable no-op in its current state); the security plugin's shared-copy-primitive hook (`Hook_CopyPrimitive`, `matchdatadone_memberjoin_fix.cpp` -- read in full, only modifies behavior for 3 exact pre-computed return addresses, everything else passes through unmodified, and `security/` had zero diff since the last confirmed-working commit); the new welcome-modal/outdated-modal system (ruled out directly -- `mw3ncp_state.ini` already had `WelcomeShownVersion` recorded, so that code path was provably skipped on the crash repro that still reproduced); a UCRT-internal `sprintf_s`-family function (`FUN_1404015f0` in `iw5mp.exe`, confirmed via a fresh Ghidra import+decompile) sits at the crash address, and the crashing thread has a genuinely small (60KB) but game's-own-design (not our) reserved stack -- neither turned out to be causal, just where the corrupted execution happened to land.

**Real root cause, found via a `git worktree` bisection** (the decisive technique -- direct user request: "maybe we need to build to check and diff from 680353b... build a build from each development day"): `680353b` (2026-09-15, last confirmed-working) launches MP cleanly; a day-by-day and then commit-by-commit bisection (`b66e5db` 09-16 broken -> `b144f685` works -> `d7b73a88` broken -> `b940ec2c` works, with `d7b73a88` its immediate next commit) isolated the exact introducing commit with no remaining ambiguity: **`d7b73a88`, "feat: port frame-pacing limiter from MW3_Standalone_D3D9_Project"**.

That commit added `OnEndSceneFramePacingX64()`, called unconditionally from `Hook_EndScene` (`overlay_hud.cpp`) -- a hook that is NOT SP-gated, unlike every gameplay hook in this codebase. It reads the game's real `com_maxfps` dvar via `GetDvarFloatX64_Exported` -> `GetDvarFloatX64` (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`) -> `FindDvarX64Raw`, which resolves `Dvar_FindVar`'s equivalent via a **hardcoded absolute address** (`0x1402c3890`), not a signature scan -- a direct violation of this project's own locked policy (`CLAUDE.md` SS5/SS10.3/SS10.8: `iw5sp.exe`/`iw5mp.exe` are separately-compiled binaries, no address carries over) that had gone unnoticed because every other dvar-reading code path in this file has always been SP-gated (part of the gameplay-hook install, MP-excluded since `game_exe_detect.h` shipped 2026-09-15) -- this was the FIRST dvar read ever to run under MP. Under `iw5mp.exe`, that fixed address points at unrelated code in that binary's own, differently-compiled layout; calling through it every frame (starting at the very first `EndScene`) executed essentially arbitrary bytes as code -- explaining every observed symptom at once: perfectly deterministic (a fixed wrong address always does the same wrong thing), MP-only, and a crash deep inside "unrelated" native code with a fixed-but-nonsensical (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF-reading, valid-memory-blaming) exception context, consistent with corrupted execution rather than a real memory-safety bug at the reported instruction.

**Fix**: `OnEndSceneFramePacingX64()` now early-returns unless `GetDetectedGameExecutable() == GameExecutable::SP`, matching the same SP-only-until-verified convention already correctly applied to the sibling wait-coalescing and `.iwd` read-cache features shipped the same day. Frame pacing simply does not run under MP until a real MP-specific signature scan for `Dvar_FindVar` exists -- not required to fix the crash, left as real future work. Build-verified and **live-confirmed by the user** ("works now") on the very next MP launch after the fix.

**Process note worth keeping**: this is the second time in two sessions a `git worktree` bisection against real anchor commits (as opposed to static code reading alone) was what actually closed out a stuck investigation -- see the 2026-08-27 motion-blur crash entry (`known_issues.md` issue #96) for the first. When static analysis and live-dump reading both plateau on a deterministic, reproducible regression, and a real "last known good" point exists, bisecting is proven, low-ambiguity, and faster than continuing to guess.


## 4. SP damage/pause/level-transition stutter -- render-scale-proportional, real hardcoded memory-pool constants found (genuine, but do not explain the full ~4GB ceiling on their own)

**Status: Investigating.** Live-reported: severe stutter on taking real (unarmored) health damage in SP, scaling with `InternalRenderScalePercent` (barely noticeable at 101%, severe at 300%) -- confirmed NOT the on-screen damage effects (isolated out), reproduces identically on the pause-menu-during-gameplay transition and on Survival level-load/camera-state transitions. User's own well-reasoned hypothesis: a hardcoded, pre-x64-recompile memory/VRAM budget (classic id-Tech Hunk/Zone allocator heritage) is still capping the engine at roughly the same ~3.8-4GB ceiling observed flat in Task Manager for both VRAM and system RAM the instant gameplay starts, and render-scale's own real VRAM cost is what's now colliding with it.

**Ruled out this session** (live diagnostic data, don't revisit): sqrt-domain-error fallback firing (zero fires); the native hurt-text-draw function being slow (normal timing); `EnsureFullscreenCaptureTexture` thrashing (only ever recreates once, at startup, at native res); `UnboundedDevLog`'s own log-volume increase being causal (user's own explicit correction -- it's a visibility setting only); "same texture recreating in a loop" for the `Hook_CreateTexture` call-volume spike (the real caller, `Create2DTexture`/`FUN_1401b8e40`, is a generic shared primitive used by the engine's own normal asset/image loader, `FUN_1401b93d0`, for loading many *different* assets during any transition -- confirmed via that function's own real error strings, not a repeated-recreate bug).

**Real, confirmed finding (static RE, `iw5sp.exe`, fresh Ghidra import -- the tracked `.rep` project under `ghidra_project_x64/` is confirmed still broken/empty, same "no files enumerate" failure noted in this issue's earlier rounds; a scratch import from `re_notes/x64_migration/binaries/iw5sp.exe` is the only working path, same workaround used previously): the classic id-Tech Hunk/Zone memory-allocator heritage genuinely exists in this binary, structurally intact. `Hunk_Alloc`-family strings (5 hits: `140435cb0`/`140435d00`/`140435d60`/`140435db0`, plus one unreferenced) resolve to a real bump allocator (`FUN_1402bd980`/`FUN_1402bda80`/`FUN_1402be4a0`/`FUN_1402bdb80`/`FUN_1402be580`) that pages memory in on demand via `VirtualAlloc(MEM_COMMIT)` as its low/high pointers advance, calling a genuine fatal-error path (`FUN_1402ee570` -> `FUN_1402eeda0`) if a commit ever fails or a pool boundary check trips -- textbook Quake3/id-Tech "Hunk_LowAlloc"/"Hunk_HighAlloc" design, not something added for x64.

Traced the base/top pointer globals (`0x14265d518`/`0x14266f240`) back to their one real writer, `FUN_1402be3d0` -- the genuine `Hunk_Init`-equivalent: `DAT_14266f240 = 0xa00000; DAT_14265d518 = VirtualAlloc(0, 0xa00000, MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_READWRITE);` -- a **hardcoded 10MB (0xa00000) reserve**, no dvar/cvar/cmdline/system-memory-query involved anywhere. **User's own sharp identification, worth recording**: 0xa00000 is exactly 10,485,760 bytes -- the exact, famous size of the Xbox 360 Xenos GPU's eDRAM (used for the tiled framebuffer on that platform). MW3 (2011) shipped cross-platform (Xbox 360/PS3/PC) from a shared codebase; this specific constant is very likely a leftover sized to match the 360's eDRAM budget for some framebuffer/tiling-related scratch use on that platform, never revisited for PC (where no such constraint exists) through any port since -- real, concrete supporting evidence for "these constants are unexamined console-era leftovers," independent of whether this specific 10MB pool turns out to be involved in the actual damage-lag mechanism. A second, structurally separate zone allocator was found the same way: `FUN_1402c9130` reserves a single `VirtualAlloc(0, 0x12c00000, MEM_RESERVE, 4)` block (~300MB) and splits it into two fixed sub-pools (`0x12a00000` / ~298MB at `DAT_142717ce0`, and `0x200000` / 2MB at the adjacent cluster) -- also fully hardcoded, no external input. A third, smaller pool (`FUN_1402be1a0`, `DAT_14265d510 = VirtualAlloc(0, 0x140000, ...)`, 1.25MB) completes the set.

All three init calls (`FUN_1402be3d0()`, `FUN_1402c9130()`, `FUN_1402be1a0()`) are invoked bare, with zero arguments, from a single real top-level function, `FUN_14023dd40` -- confirmed via full decompile to be the genuine `Com_Init`-equivalent (parses `+`-separated command-line tokens, execs `default.cfg`/`config.cfg`, dvar-restart handling, build-version string, etc.). **No call anywhere in this chain to `GlobalMemoryStatusEx`, `GetPhysicallyInstalledSystemMemory`, or any other system-memory-query API** -- these pool sizes are not adaptive to installed RAM/VRAM in any way, on either architecture. This is genuine, confirmed evidence that the engine's CPU-side memory subsystem is exactly as static as the user's hypothesis predicted: whatever was hardcoded in the original 32-bit-era binary carried through the x64 recompile completely unexamined.

**Important, honest scope correction**: these three pools sum to roughly 311MB total (10MB + ~300MB + 1.25MB) -- nowhere near the ~3.8-4GB ceiling the user observed live in Task Manager. This RE pass does NOT identify a single hardcoded constant that explains that specific figure. Two real possibilities going forward, not yet distinguished: (1) the ~4GB figure is a **D3D9/GPU-side** texture-memory-pool or working-set ceiling, a completely separate subsystem from this CPU-side `Com_Init` chain (device/texture creation happens far later, driven by the renderer's own init, not traced this session) -- the more likely candidate given the number is VRAM-shaped, not RAM-shaped; or (2) it's an OS/driver-level default (e.g. a WDDM budget notification the engine never queries or reacts to, so it just runs into it) rather than anything hardcoded in this binary at all. The render-scale-proportional stutter itself is still unexplained by what's been found so far -- these hardcoded CPU pools are confirmed real and confirmed unrelated to x64 adaptation, but not yet confirmed as *the* mechanism behind the reported lag.

**10MB Hunk consumer traced (same session, follow-up)**: checked whether the 10MB pool's real Xbox 360 eDRAM-size coincidence extended to actual usage -- i.e. whether it holds render-command/tiling-adjacent data on PC, a leftover from wherever it lived on 360. Traced all real callers of the Hunk-alloc functions (`FUN_1402bd980`/`FUN_1402bda80`/`FUN_1402be4a0`/`FUN_1402bdb80`/`FUN_1402be580`, ~9 distinct call sites): string interning (`FUN_1402b2360`, a hash-bucket string-pool cache used broadly across the engine), animation-script parsing (`mp/playeranimtypes.txt` via `BG_AnimParseAnimScript`), AI-type GSC script assignment (`aitype/%s`, `misc_mg42`/`misc_turret`, `GScr_SetScriptAndLabel`), and -- notably -- the hardware auto-config routine (`configure.csv` parsing, followed by `exec options_graphics.cfg` / `vid_restart` / `snd_restart`). **Every single traced consumer is ordinary text/string/script scratch work, none render-command or GPU-adjacent.** Consistent with the call site itself (`VirtualAlloc(..., PAGE_READWRITE)`, no D3D9 involvement anywhere in the chain) -- eDRAM on 360 lived on the GPU die, reachable only through Xenos-specific tiling/resolve APIs, never through a generic C-level `Hunk_Alloc`. Read together: the 10MB size match to 360's eDRAM is very likely a genuine numeric coincidence (or a case of someone picking a round number they had 360's memory budget in mind for) rather than this pool having ever literally held eDRAM-bound data -- it's a generic scratch Hunk, on this evidence always has been. Doesn't change the broader "untouched console-era constant" reading at all, just narrows what this specific 10MB pool is actually for.

**Cross-binary confirmation (same session, earlier round)**: re-ran the same trace against `iw5mp.exe` -- a completely separately-compiled binary (per this project's own SS10.8, no offset/constant is assumed to carry over between the two exes) -- and found byte-for-byte identical hardcoded reserves: `VirtualAlloc(0, 0xa00000, MEM_RESERVE, 4)` (same 10MB Hunk) and `VirtualAlloc(0, 0x12c00000, MEM_RESERVE, 4)` (same ~300MB Zone, same `0x200000`/2MB sub-pool split). Two independently-built executables carrying the exact same numbers is strong, concrete confirmation of the user's own reading: these constants are not per-binary-tuned, let alone per-platform-tuned -- they come from shared engine source that has gone completely untouched and has simply been repurposed wholesale on every port since, PC included. (MP does have one additional/divergent pool not present in SP's traced set, `DAT_146b49168 = VirtualAlloc(0, 0x200000, ...)`, plausibly MP-specific netcode buffer space -- not yet traced further, noted for completeness only.)

**~300MB Zone consumer traced (same session, follow-up)**: user hypothesized this pool might be a dormant Xbox 360-built texture buffer. Traced the real allocator built on top of it (`FUN_1402c8e30`, a per-thread-indexed bump-with-VirtualAlloc-commit function, keyed by a render/job-thread index from `FUN_1400a6410`/`FUN_1400a5fd0`) up through its real callers. Found it is **genuinely, actively used, not dormant**: `FUN_1400a8090` (the real caller chain's root) builds a `"%s.ff"` filename, opens it via `FUN_1402cca30`, and carries a `"MENU_CONTENT_NOT_AVAILABLE"` error string -- this is the real **FastFile (.ff zone archive) loader**, the classic id-Tech content-Zone consumer. Two sibling functions (`FUN_140244510`/`FUN_14023f540`) also draw large fixed chunks from the same zone at startup (`0xf218`/`0x2f440` bytes) to pre-carve arrays of fixed-size (`0x790`-byte) structs, consistent with the classic id-Tech "many subsystems each grab a permanent chunk from the shared content Zone" pattern.

**Correction, not the user's exact framing but closely related**: this is the genuine, live, actively-used content Zone -- the CPU-side pool loaded `.ff` FastFile *content* (materials, structs, and other subsystem data referenced by loaded zones) lives in -- not raw texture pixel data itself, which is uploaded separately via `CreateTexture`/D3D9 into actual GPU VRAM, a completely different allocator this trace hasn't touched. So "texture buffer" isn't quite right, but "console-era zone sized once and never revisited, now a fixed ~300MB ceiling on how much loaded-level content can live in memory at once regardless of how much RAM the PC actually has" is exactly the same shape of problem, and IS a real, concrete, plausible contributor: if a damage/pause/level-transition event triggers the FastFile loader to stream in more zone content than usual while this fixed pool is already under pressure, the repeated `VirtualAlloc(MEM_COMMIT)` calls inside `FUN_1402c8e30` (or, in the worst case, the `FUN_1402eeda0(7)` fatal-exhaustion path) are a real, plausible stutter/lag mechanism -- worth keeping as an active theory alongside the D3D9/GPU-side VRAM-ceiling theory, not instead of it.

**Next step**: the live `ResourceUsageLogging=1` diagnostic (already enabled in the deployed `mw3ncp_config.ini` this session, not yet tested) logs real process working-set/private-bytes/pagefile usage once a second -- a live capture during a damage-lag repro at high render scale is the natural next data point, since it can show whether working-set/commit actually approaches a hard ceiling at the moment the stutter hits, which would point toward (1) or (2) above (or this Zone specifically) more concretely than further static RE can.

**Live CPU-side resource-diag capture, real data (same session, follow-up)**: a real `ResourceUsageLogging`/`FrametimeBenchmarkLogging` capture during actual Campaign play (the Act 1 airplane mission, live-reported at 19fps vs. Survival's 60fps at identical settings, `InternalRenderScalePercent=300` confirmed still set -- true 7680x4320/8K internal render target, confirmed via the `[overlay-hud][res-scale]` log lines) showed `ourOwnTotalMs` near-zero (0.001-0.005ms) on every one of 1114 logged "SLOW FRAME" entries (94-101ms each, ~10fps) with `realCreateTextureMs=0.000 calls=0` -- this project's own hooks are not the bottleneck for this specific symptom. `privateBytesMB` (CPU-side process commit, NOT GPU VRAM) over the full session ranged from 206MB at launch up to a real peak of 4857.7MB, dropped sharply to ~3235MB (a real level/zone-transition content release, consistent with this issue's own traced FastFile-zone-loader finding above), then climbed back to a ~4172-4247MB plateau during the low-fps mission itself -- genuinely dynamic, content-driven behavior, NOT a flat/rigid ceiling repeatedly hit. This significantly weakens (does not disprove) the CPU-side-hardcoded-pool theory as the PRIMARY driver of the low framerate specifically; true 8K rendering in a GPU/overdraw-heavy scripted scene is a real, sufficient, mundane explanation on its own, independent of any console-era memory constant.

**Real GPU VRAM diagnostics added (same session, follow-up)**: user's own sharp counter-observation -- at confirmed `InternalRenderScalePercent=300` (true 8K), observed VRAM usage (Task Manager) never exceeds ~3.8GB, suspiciously low for that resolution if nothing were capping it. Two diagnostics added to `Hook_EndScene` (`overlay_hud.cpp`), rate-limited ~1s each: (1) the legacy `IDirect3DDevice9::GetAvailableTextureMemory` (now explicitly labeled unreliable in its own log line -- this is a well-known, driver-fudged legacy D3D9 API most vendors report conservatively through, not a trustworthy live gauge); (2) a new, real, authoritative diagnostic via `IDXGIAdapter3::QueryVideoMemoryInfo` (new file `vram_diag.cpp`/`.h`, `dxgi.lib` linked) -- the same per-process VRAM budget/usage accounting Windows' own Task Manager GPU memory tab and GPU-Z actually use, querying the `DXGI_MEMORY_SEGMENT_GROUP_LOCAL` segment's real `Budget`/`CurrentUsage`. Deliberately resolves adapter 0 (default/primary GPU) rather than LUID-matching the live D3D9 device -- correct for the overwhelming majority of single-GPU systems this project tests against, flagged as a known simplification for multi-GPU setups, not a silent gap. Both x64 and Win32 build-verified, x64 redeployed last.

**CRITICAL, same-day**: the legacy diagnostic's own new log line crashed the game on first real launch (`sprintf_s<128>` `FAST_FAIL_INVALID_ARG`, `c0000409`, confirmed via static `mcp-windbg` analysis of `iw5sp.exe.24228.dmp` -- no live attach, per this project's own standing rule) -- **the SIXTH real occurrence of this exact recurring bug class** (2026-09-05, twice on 2026-09-13/14, 2026-09-16, once earlier on 2026-09-17, now this): a ~150-byte worst-case message sized into a 128-byte buffer. Fixed with real, generous margin (256 bytes, not a bare fit), plus a proactive sweep of the new `vram_diag.cpp`'s own two `sprintf_s` calls for the same risk (the adapter-description line had only ~8 bytes of margin over its own real ~392-byte worst case -- widened to 640). No new lesson beyond what's already on record; the standing "per-commit discipline, not a periodic sweep" rule was simply skipped again for a brand-new call site. Build-verified, redeployed; not yet re-confirmed live by the user as of this entry.

**Real DXGI VRAM data, live-confirmed (same session, follow-up)**: a real capture (RTX 2080 Ti) showed `budgetMB` flat at 10259.0 (~10.26GB) the entire session while `currentUsageMB` ranged only 1020.5-2621.5MB -- roughly 7.6GB of real, unused VRAM headroom throughout, even at 300%/8K. This conclusively rules out a VRAM ceiling as the cause of any of this symptom family. Zero `[createtexture-storm-diag]` entries the same session -- also rules out a texture-creation storm.

**Direct user report, same session: ADS engagement ALSO produces a sustained ~2x FPS drop, GPU usage confirmed FLAT throughout (Afterburner, live-monitored) -- not just damage/pause/level-transitions.** Generalizes the whole symptom family beyond damage specifically. Chased and ruled out in order: the in-mod frame pacer (`com_maxfps` confirmed reading `0`/inert the entire session -- `OnEndSceneFramePacingX64`'s blocking wait never ran once); RTSS and Afterburner both closed for a control test -- drop persists, ruling both out; real vsync -- confirmed off for every test (x86's own precedent for this exact symptom class, issue #99, doesn't apply here); this session's own new VRAM diagnostic calls -- direct timing added, only one real cost found (a one-time 19ms DXGI factory-creation call at launch, nothing recurring) -- cleared. **User's own direct, decisive isolation test: render scale confirmed the SOLE factor** (motion blur specifically ruled out live, all other visual-suite toggles left on) -- and, critically, **x86 never showed this symptom at 250% render scale**, ruling out "any high render scale saturates any GPU" as a sufficient explanation on its own and pointing at something specific to the x64 port/binary.

**Dispatch-table trace, same session -- a real, strong candidate mechanism found.** Re-traced the real per-frame readers of the RESOLVED_SCENE/backbuffer surface globals (`DAT_141bb6e28`/`DAT_14188bc10`) beyond the single previously-documented Present-time StretchRect (`FUN_14018b840`) and found two more real per-frame consumers never traced before: `FUN_14018b6c0` and `FUN_1401d4f60`. Both callers of `FUN_14018b6c0` resolved to DATA references (not direct calls) landing in `DAT_14040e630` -- the exact jump table `FUN_140189940`'s own confirmed `while(*p!=0){ jumpTable[*p](&p); }` dispatch loop indexes into (the SAME per-viewport 2D/HUD command-stream architecture this project's motion-blur trigger already hooks off of). Index math: `(0x14040e698 - 0x14040e630) / 8 = 13` -- **`FUN_14018b6c0` is opcode 13** in this real command stream, not a fixed per-frame call.

Its real body (full decompile on file, `re_notes/ghidra_scripts`) is a genuine SCALAR, PER-PIXEL CPU copy loop: `LockRect` a fresh offscreen surface sized to a sub-rectangle, hand-copy every pixel with a byte-order shuffle (no SIMD, no GPU work) in a nested row/column loop, `UnlockRect`, then `StretchRect` the result into the real backbuffer at a specific screen position. Real CPU cost scaling with `width * height` -- i.e. render-scale SQUARED, not linear (200% render scale = 4x the pixel count of native for this specific command alone). This is a mechanistically exact match for every confirmed symptom at once: no GPU usage spike (pure CPU work, would never show there), a real cost multiplier tied directly to render-scale percent, and plausible correlation with UI/state-transition-style moments (pause, an ADS scope overlay, a mission-specific screen effect) that would queue this specific opcode -- unlike the already-ruled-out hurt-text/sqrt-domain-error chain, this isn't damage-specific by construction, consistent with the ADS finding generalizing the symptom.

A pure diagnostic hook (`Hook_ScreenCaptureCmdDiag`, zero behavior change, always calls through) was built and deployed on `FUN_14018b6c0` -- logs every real fire's width/height and call duration, no rate limit (a real opcode-gated command should be rare, not per-frame; if it turns out to fire every frame instead, that itself is important data). Signature built from raw disassembly (111 bytes; only two real position-dependent operands, a RIP-relative load and a `JS rel32`, both wildcarded -- the rest of the tool's own "PC-relative" flags in this span are the same false-positive class (`kPmoveTickSignature`'s R11-relative-stack-displacement note) this file already documents, confirmed via manual review, not assumed). x64-only file, build-verified, deployed.

**Live-tested, RULED OUT (same session, follow-up):** a real capture at confirmed 300% (`7680x4320` logged) produced ZERO fires of opcode 13 -- `FUN_14018b6c0` never ran once. Cleanly rules this specific opcode out as the mechanism.

**Real repro data instead pointed at a different, more severe symptom: an explosion-into-downed-state transition, confirmed by the user as the single most severe lag trigger of all repros tested.** The same capture showed two multi-second stalls (1956ms, 2393ms) directly correlating with a genuine `CreateTexture` storm (1116/1779 calls) and real disk reads -- but the real measured cost (this project's own hooks + actual `CreateTexture` time, 52ms/115ms) accounted for barely 5% of each stall, leaving the vast majority genuinely unaccounted for. The storm dump's own caller-ID (a single `_ReturnAddress()`) attributed every one of the 292 calls in a separate capture to the same address -- confirmed to be `FUN_1401b8e40` (`Create2DTexture`), the one generic wrapper every real texture creation funnels through regardless of the actual requesting subsystem, making the single-frame version unable to identify what's really responsible. Upgraded to a real short stack walk (`CaptureStackBackTrace`, 6 frames, a genuine fast/safe kernel32 export) so the dump shows frames past the generic wrapper into the real calling subsystem -- not yet live-tested under real repro conditions.

**Direct cross-reference to x86's OWN already-documented finding, confirmed as the same architecture on x64 (known_issues.md issue #88):** x86's RE established that render targets split into two independently-sized pools -- `DAT_021d2e00/04` (unclamped, render-scale-driven, feeds the real scene/post-effect chain) and `DAT_021d2e08/0c` (quality-TIER-CLAMPED, discrete steps `0x500x0x2d0`=**1280x720** / `0x640x??`=1600 / `0x780x??`=1920, capped to native) -- and the tier-clamped pair feeds exactly ONE thing: `R_RENDERTARGET_SAVED_SCREEN`, a screenshot/thumbnail capture buffer, completely independent of render scale. This is a DIRECT match for the fixed `1280x720`/`1024x1024` CreateTexture-storm entries found this session. x64 mirrors the identical split (confirmed via this session's own earlier decompile of `FUN_1401d44f0`): `DAT_141888670/674` (unclamped) feeds the real chain, `DAT_141888678/67c` (tier-clamped) feeds SAVED_SCREEN only. Leading theory: the downed-state transition triggers a screen capture into this small, fixed-tier buffer (a classic "freeze/desaturate the screen" effect), and that capture's real cost scales with the huge SOURCE resolution (the full supersampled scene) being resolved down into the small fixed destination -- explaining the render-scale-proportional severity, the correlation with a real state-transition event, and the fixed sizes in the storm dump all at once.

Traced the real consumers of the SAVED_SCREEN globals (`DAT_141bb6e00/08/18/1c`) and decompiled the strongest candidate, `FUN_1401dfd80` -- found to be the generic "activate render view N" dispatcher (x64 equivalent of x86's own documented `FUN_0049bf50`), called with a different index per render target/pass, not SAVED_SCREEN-specific in isolation. Added a pure diagnostic hook (`Hook_RenderViewSelectDiag`, zero behavior change) logging on view-index CHANGES only, to see the real activation sequence and whether SAVED_SCREEN's own index appears unusually often specifically during the explosion/downed-state moment. Signature built from raw disassembly (108 bytes, two real wildcarded jump-target operands, the rest confirmed-literal stack-spill stores). x64-only file, build-verified, deployed.

**Real SAVED_SCREEN capture function found and decompiled in full, same session, follow-up: `FUN_14018a780`.** Confirms the leading theory exactly: `StretchRect(currentActiveViewSurface -> SAVED_SCREEN surface, filter=linear)`, gated by a per-consumer generation-staleness check (`if (DAT_141887e20[consumerIdx] != DAT_1415e9438) { capture(); DAT_141887e20[consumerIdx] = DAT_1415e9438; }`) -- a genuine downsample from the full render-scale-driven active view down into the small, fixed-tier SAVED_SCREEN destination, exactly matching the cross-referenced x86 architecture. Searched all 6 real reference sites to `DAT_1415e9438` (the shared generation counter) for its writer -- none of the 6 write it (all read/compare/stamp only), meaning the actual increment site sits in code not yet disassembled under this scoped `-noanalysis` pass; left as a secondary, unresolved detail since the capture mechanism itself is now fully confirmed regardless of exactly what drives the counter.

**First real fix attempt shipped, per direct user instruction ("no live diags unless i state that or agree... id like to attempt fixes"):** `Hook_SavedScreenCaptureFix` on `FUN_14018a780` -- rather than reimplementing the capture/blit logic (real risk of a wrong struct-field-offset or D3D9 refcounting detail), pre-writes the current generation value into the specific consumer's own staleness stamp before calling the real trampoline when `InternalRenderScalePercent > 150` (matching the same threshold `Hook_RenderResCompute`'s own high-scale warning already uses), making the engine's OWN staleness check see "already up to date" and skip its own capture path using its existing logic. A genuine no-op below the threshold -- the real trampoline runs completely unmodified at default/near-native render scale. Honest, undischarged tradeoff: SAVED_SCREEN shows stale/last-good content instead of a fresh capture while active above 150% -- the exact visual scope isn't fully mapped (read by several real subsystems: the render-view dispatcher, the hurt-text draw path, the scene-finish orchestrator, among others per this session's own trace), so confirming nothing looks visually wrong needs a real playtest, not something static RE alone can settle. Signature built from raw disassembly (199 bytes, six real wildcarded operands -- four RIP-relative loads, one CALL rel32, one JZ rel8/rel32 pair -- the rest confirmed-literal, including two RBP-relative-to-imagebase accesses with stable link-time RVA displacements that don't need wildcarding). x64-only file, build-verified, deployed.

**LIVE-TESTED, RULED OUT: fix #1 had zero effect on the reported lag.** Confirmed via log that the hook genuinely installed and engaged (render scale confirmed at real 300%/8K during the test), yet the symptom was unchanged -- a real, clean negative result. Either `FUN_14018a780` isn't firing during this specific repro, or SAVED_SCREEN was never the dominant mechanism. Per direct user instruction ("keep pushin" statically, no more live diags without agreement), pivoted to a completely different angle.

**REAL ROOT CAUSE FOUND: a hardcoded 3072MB (3GB) system-memory detection cap, confirmed via a live config-edit test plus full decompile.** Direct user reframing: "im guessing... this is probably some form of internal engine limit on my particular hardware" -- matching the user's own very first hypothesis from the start of this whole investigation. `players2/config.cfg` showed `seta sys_sysMB "3072"` with `com_recommendedSet "1"` (the hardware auto-benchmark already run and locked in). **Live config-edit test**: changed `sys_sysMB` to the real detected system RAM (28265MB) directly in the live config file -- on the very next launch, it was silently reverted back to `3072`, **with `sys_configSum` also resetting from a real checksum to `0`** -- definitive proof the engine actively RE-RUNS its own hardware detection every launch and consistently recomputes the same wrong value, not a stale cached number from some earlier run.

Traced the real writer (not a simple string-keyed dvar write -- found via the cached dvar pointer `DAT_14279dd10` instead): `FUN_1402ef150`/`FUN_1402eded0` both call `SetDvarInt(sys_sysMB, DAT_14279dac8)`, and `DAT_14279dac8 = FUN_1402ea710()` -- the real hardware-memory-detection function. Full decompile of `FUN_1402ea710` confirms the exact bug: it correctly calls the real `GlobalMemoryStatusEx`/`GlobalMemoryStatus` APIs and computes a genuine MB value from actual detected system RAM -- then unconditionally clamps it: `if (((float)iVar1 * DAT_1403fcbd8 < (float)local_98.dwTotalPhys) || (0xc00 < iVar1)) { iVar1 = 0xc00; }`. **`0xc00` is 3072 decimal** -- a real, confirmed, unchanged-since-32-bit-era hardcoded 3GB ceiling on detected system memory, throwing away the real value for any system with more RAM (virtually every system built in the last 15 years). `sys_sysMB` then feeds the already-traced hardware-tier auto-detect logic (`FUN_1401b9980`/`FUN_1401b9d50`) that drives internal engine quality/budget decisions.

**Fix #2 shipped**: `Hook_MemDetectFix`, a POST-hook on `FUN_1402ea710` -- the real trampoline runs completely unmodified first (preserving its own legitimate low-memory-warning dialog for genuinely low-RAM systems, and leaving any real sub-3072MB result untouched), and only when the result is EXACTLY `0xc00` (the precise signature of the cap firing, not a coincidentally real 3072MB system) does it override with a real, freshly-computed, uncapped value from this project's own `GlobalMemoryStatusEx` call, bounded to the dvar's own real `INT32_MAX` registration ceiling. Signature built from raw disassembly (35-byte function-entry prefix only, not the full 154-byte body -- the function is dense with real message-box/string-load RIP-relative operands, so a minimal, safely-unique entry signature was used instead of risking an incomplete wildcard map over the whole body). x64-only file, build-verified, deployed.

**LIVE-TESTED, RULED OUT: fix #2 also had zero effect.** Same clean negative result as fix #1 -- the cap correction is real and confirmed working (per the fix's own log line), but the symptom is unchanged.

**Fourth angle tested, also ruled out live: `WaitCoalescingEnabled=0`** (an existing, already-shipped x64-exclusive feature with zero x86 equivalent -- `wait_coalescing_x64.cpp`, deliberately stretches the render thread's own `Sleep(1)`/`WaitForSingleObject(1)` polling calls up to 2-4ms during a detected disk-I/O burst). A strong theoretical match for every observed symptom (pure CPU-side, event-gated, x64-only) -- disabled live via config, **zero change** to the reported lag.

**Fifth angle traced statically, also ruled out: the full-render-scale POST_EFFECT_0/1 buffers' real consumers.** Direct user correction mid-investigation ("ive told you 11000% its guaranteed a render increase causation") redirected the search to the actual render pipeline rather than I/O/hardware-detection tangents. Found two real, previously-unexamined consumer functions (`FUN_140189c90`/`FUN_140189ed0`) touching both POST_EFFECT buffers directly -- but full decompile showed these are shader-sampler/constant-TABLE setup (registering which texture binds to named samplers like `"postEffect0"`/`"postEffect1"`), not a draw call. Traced both of their real callers to ground: one resolves to the already-known hardware-tier detection chain (`FUN_1401b9980` -> `FUN_1401976a0`), the other to the confirmed once-per-process device-creation orchestrator (`FUN_1401bcf30`, early-return-guarded). Both are genuine one-time startup init, not a per-frame or per-event draw -- this specific angle is exhausted via static tracing alone.

**Current working conclusion (2026-09-23), direct user synthesis**: with the mod's own render-scale override mechanism confirmed to work symmetrically in both directions (the same `Hook_RenderResCompute` override applies whether the target is above OR below native -- the only real constraint is the engine's own 640x480 floor, e.g. 25% at 2560x1440 native computes to 640x360 and silently fails that floor on height alone, while ~34%+ clears it cleanly) and every mod-side theory now eliminated via direct live testing (SAVED_SCREEN capture, the sys_sysMB cap, wait coalescing) or exhaustive static tracing (the POST_EFFECT setup functions, the opcode-13 CPU pixel-copy loop, the generic CreateTexture/asset-loader chain), the most evidence-consistent remaining explanation is a **genuine native engine stability characteristic tied to large render-target/texture sizes specifically**, not a bug in this project's own code or hooking mechanism. Direct user theory, plausible but not independently provable from RE alone: this is very likely *why* the original PC port's internal render resolution was locked to a fixed reference size (1920x1080 default, tier-clamped `SAVED_SCREEN` at 1280x720) regardless of actual display/backbuffer size in the first place (issue #88's own original 2026-08-25 finding) -- a genuine, real stability boundary the original developers already knew about and engineered around, that this project's own `InternalRenderScalePercent` supersampling feature (by design, deliberately uncapped above native, see issue #88's "REAL fix" entry) reopens by construction whenever pushed far enough above what the engine was ever validated at. Consistent with, not contradicted by, the real x86-era precedent this session cross-referenced (issue #105): x86 had its own real crashes/freezes above 250% too, though that specific case's root cause (a `ForceD3D9On12`-driven lingering driver corruption) was different and that feature has since been removed entirely -- the underlying "high render scale is where this engine's real stability envelope ends" pattern recurring independently on both architectures, via different specific mechanisms, is itself supporting evidence for a genuine engine-level rather than mod-code-level boundary.

**Practical implication, not yet actioned**: if this conclusion holds, the productive path forward is likely narrowing the actual SAFE maximum `InternalRenderScalePercent` (confirmed clean at 200%, confirmed broken at 300%, exact boundary between the two not yet tested) rather than continuing to hunt for a single patchable bug -- a real, bounded next step if resumed, not a technical dead end.

**MP visual-suite port scoping (2026-09-23)**, direct instruction: "okay time to make the graphics enhancements available on mp so we have a few feats for this release." Signature-scanned all four candidate hook/gate targets against `iw5mp.exe` (`PatternScanMP.java`, a new Ghidra headless script written this session): `kRenderResComputeSignature` (render scale) -> **1 clean match** @ `0x1401e2e00`; `kMotionBlurTriggerSignature` -> **1 clean match** @ `0x1401b3e40`; `kFindDvarX64Signature` -> **1 clean match** @ `0x140324270`; `kInLevelFlagSignature` (one of FSR/motion blur's three required safety gates, per the hard-won issue #103/#104 crash-history policy) -> **0 matches**. Render scale's own hook body (`Hook_RenderResCompute`) only reads `g_modConfig.internalRenderScalePercent` and writes into the caller-supplied struct pointer -- no dependency on `g_menuActiveGateFlag`/`g_inLevelFlag`/anything else SP-only-resolved -- so it was split out into its own `InstallRenderScaleHookX64()` (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`) and wired into both the SP and MP branches in `dllmain.cpp`. Motion blur/FSR were NOT ported despite their own trigger/dvar-lookup signatures resolving cleanly -- their shared in-level gate has zero matches under `iw5mp.exe`, and shipping either without all three proven-necessary gates would repeat the exact mistake issues #103/#104 already paid for once. The forced-quality dvar toggles (`ForceAnisotropicFiltering`/`ForceHighQualityShadows`/`ForceHighQualityLighting`) were also considered and excluded -- investigating them surfaced a separate, deeper, pre-existing bug (they're silent no-ops on x64 entirely, SP included, not something this port introduced or is blocked by) -- see issue #6. Build-verified both platforms, x64 redeployed last; not yet live-tested against a real `iw5mp.exe` session. Commit `8cedba45`.

**HUGE live-test finding, MP, same day, first real playtest of the port above**: at exactly 200% -- the threshold SP confirmed CLEAN at, no stutter at all -- **MP lags constantly, at all times, not gated to any specific trigger event.** Direct user report: "at just 200% on mp that lag is present at all times. this is exactly what i expected and most likely why it was restricted like it was." This is a materially different symptom shape from SP's own repro (damage/pause/ADS/level-transition/explosion-downed-state -- discrete, event-triggered spikes, otherwise "TOO smooth" per the user's own earlier live description) -- MP's own cost is apparently CONTINUOUS at the same render-scale percentage SP tolerates cleanly, not event-gated at all. Direct user theory, and the most evidence-consistent reading of everything this investigation has found so far: **this is the same genuine native engine stability/cost boundary already concluded above, just made visible sooner because MP's own per-frame workload (more simultaneous players, more concurrently-rendered weapon/character models, more active netcode/prediction state, generally busier scenes than SP's own more controlled encounter design) sits closer to that boundary BEFORE any render-scale multiplier is even applied** -- consistent with the user's own direct follow-on prediction: "its clear not all maps, modes etc stress the engine anywhere near the same rate so some may run fine while others may be 4x less performant." In other words, the real safe `InternalRenderScalePercent` ceiling isn't a single fixed number at all -- it's content-dependent, and MP as a class (denser scenes generally) likely sits meaningfully lower than SP's own tested 200%-clean/300%-broken boundary, with real per-map/per-mode variance on top of that. This doesn't overturn anything already concluded (the underlying "large render-target size is a genuine engine stability boundary, not a mod-code bug" finding) -- it sharpens it: what's actually variable is HOW MUCH headroom above native a given piece of content has before hitting that same boundary, not whether the boundary itself is real.

**CORRECTION, real, same-day re-examination (following the Campaign heli-sequence/`com_maxfps` investigation elsewhere in this issue): the "denser MP scenes/more players" theory above does NOT actually hold up.** Direct user clarification, when asked whether the constant-MP-lag finding above had been re-tested in a low-population private match: "that was that test back then" -- **the original MP lag test WAS ALREADY a private match**, not a populated public lobby. This removes the one piece of evidence the "more simultaneous players/denser scenes" explanation was actually built on -- a private match has minimal real population/entity load, essentially the same order of magnitude as SP's own "controlled encounter design," yet still showed CONSTANT (not event-gated) lag at 200%. **The population-density explanation is therefore wrong, or at minimum unproven and likely wrong** -- something about `iw5mp.exe` ITSELF (a genuine binary/build difference from `iw5sp.exe`, independent of how many real players/entities are actually in the match) is the more evidence-consistent explanation now. This is a real, useful narrowing, not a dead end: it rules out "just add more render-scale headroom margin for busier MP content" as the right mental model, and points back toward the same open question raised by the user's own separate "but it doesn't explain the exact same symptom on MP too" pushback on the scripted-event-density theory -- something x64-recompile-specific and NOT content-density-driven is the common thread across SP's pause-menu tragedy, SP's scripted-event bursts, and MP's constant lag alike. Real, not yet actioned: this reopens the question of what's actually different about the `iw5mp.exe` binary's own render/tick path vs `iw5sp.exe`'s, a genuine RE target rather than an "expected content cost" explanation to file away.

**Real synthesis, same day, direct user framing: "something changed on x64 from x86 draw pipeline which fundamentally broke the perf of the engine despite having the chance to actually make this engine run wild fast... not our work but the game."** The cleanest theory yet to actually fit every data point gathered across this whole investigation without contradiction, and it already has real supporting evidence on record in this SAME file rather than being a fresh guess: **"x86 never showed this symptom at 250% render scale"** (the original 2026-09-23 render-scale investigation's own live A/B comparison, same reference hardware) -- direct, existing proof x86's own draw pipeline tolerated heavy supersampling fine, meaning the x64 recompile specifically regressed something in how draw work gets submitted/dispatched, not "large render targets are just inherently expensive on this engine" as the standing conclusion had assumed. Every other finding in this issue is consistent with "the x64 draw pipeline itself is the common cost driver, not content or scripting": pause menu (simulation halted, zero script/entity cost) is still tragic -> can only be the render path; the SP heli sequence is worse than calmer scripted moments -> more camera/draw submission work compounding on the same regressed pipeline; MP shows constant lag even in a private/low-population match (per the correction immediately above) -> not population density, the SAME regressed pipeline running under a different binary. Real, concrete next RE target this points at (not yet started): the render command-buffer/dispatch architecture this same session already mapped for the first time (`renderer_architecture_map.md`, the frontend/backend split, `FUN_1401d2930`'s ring-buffer command submission) -- the most likely real hiding place for a genuine x64-specific regression in HOW draw commands get issued/dispatched, as opposed to what they draw. A true side-by-side x86-vs-x64 comparison against the SAME current content isn't trivially available (the x86 line is frozen against the pre-recompile retail build, and a real downgrader tool exists per issue #8's Reddit thread but only partially works per its own OP's report) -- the existing 250% x86 data point above is the best real comparative evidence on record until/unless that's revisited.

**LIVE-TESTED, real and significant confirmation, 2026-09-24: a genuine dedicated render/backend thread exists on x64, and losing it correlates directly with the worst frame spikes observed.** A cheap diagnostic (`[render-thread-diag]`, `Hook_EndScene` vs. `g_mainThreadId`, see `renderer_architecture_map.md` section 6 for the full record) confirmed `EndScene` genuinely runs on a real, distinct, persistent second thread for the overwhelming majority of a session, NOT the main thread -- closing a real, previously-unanswered architectural question in the affirmative, not by static guesswork but by direct live observation. **The real find**: across the session, `EndScene`'s calling thread flipped back to the main thread exactly twice, and BOTH times the very next frame spiked to 100-165ms (vs. a normal ~16-35ms) before flipping back and normal framerate resuming. Two independent occurrences of the identical pattern. One candidate correlate (`ShouldDrawGlyphOverlay()`'s `overlayOn` flag) was checked and ruled out as ambient/always-true state, not a real trigger -- a real negative result, not silently dropped. A genuine, not-yet-confirmed candidate found instead: both switches are immediately preceded by a burst of rapid `x64-renderview-select-diag` view-index changes, a real non-ambient signal. **This is now the single strongest, most concrete lead in this whole investigation** -- a genuine thread-handoff cost, directly observed correlating with the worst spikes, rather than an inferred content/scripting/population theory. Real next step: identify what native condition drives that view-index burst (trace `x64-renderview-select-diag`'s own call site), and correlate a future capture against actual player action at the exact frame numbers where it recurs.

**Practical implication for the on-screen 200% warning (Hook_RenderResCompute, both SP and MP now share this code path via `InstallRenderScaleHookX64()` above)**: the current warning text is SP-authored ("clean at 200%, broken at 300%... on this project's own reference GPU") and, per this finding, is now confirmed NOT accurate for MP specifically -- MP's own real safe ceiling is evidently lower than 200%, not the same number reused across both binaries. Not yet actioned -- flagged here rather than silently patched, since the right fix (a genuinely separate, lower, and likely still content-dependent MP threshold/wording, vs. widening the existing SP warning's own language to caveat that MP's real ceiling may be meaningfully lower) is a real design decision, not a mechanical one-line change.

**Further real live data, same day, under `GraphicsApi=Vulkan` at 200%: the same content-dependence generalizes across BOTH backends, not just SP-vs-MP.** Following the "game runs amazing now on vulkan at 120-140 fps" report (issue #2's newest round), direct follow-up: "though again that campaign mission is significantly slower (runs at about 30-32 fps constant)" -- the same Act 1 airplane-mission-class heavy scripted sequence this file's own earlier round already flagged as the most severe SP repro (19fps under `LegacyD3D9` at 300%) still runs meaningfully worse than this project's own typical 120-140fps Vulkan baseline, even under Vulkan and even at the lower, SP-clean 200% setting -- a real, sustained ~30-32fps floor, not an event-gated spike. This is consistent with, not contradicted by, the standing conclusion above: DXVK's own Vulkan present path clearly avoids whatever D3D9-specific stutter causes this project spent significant effort chasing under `LegacyD3D9` (hence the dramatically better general-case framerate), but it does NOT raise the underlying engine-level content-cost ceiling itself -- a genuinely GPU/overdraw-heavy scripted sequence is still genuinely GPU/overdraw-heavy regardless of which backend translates the draw calls. Real, not yet actioned: no fix attempted or warranted here, this is expected, content-driven cost, not a bug -- recorded as a further data point for the same "the real safe ceiling is content-dependent, not one fixed number" finding this issue already established for SP-vs-MP.

**`com_maxfps` hard-cap theory tested live and cleanly DISPROVEN, same day.** Direct user hypothesis on the ~30-32fps floor above: "its stuck at 30fps(maybe deliberate port setup by activision, physics etc can break)... very very much looks like com_maxfps" -- a real, well-reasoned theory (level-scoped framerate caps to protect scripted-sequence/physics timing are a genuine, precedented technique in this engine family). Tested via a real, safe, zero-behavior-change diagnostic: `OnEndSceneFramePacingX64`'s own existing `[frame-pacing-diag] com_maxfps changed -> N` log line was previously gated BEHIND the `framePacingEnabled` early-return (dead with pacing off, its default state) -- moved above both early-returns (still SP-only-gated, matching the exact same MP-unsafe-hardcoded-`GetDvarFloatX64` constraint this function's own crash-fix comment already documents) so it logs the real native `com_maxfps` value every time it changes, unconditionally, without engaging the actual limiter. `FrametimeBenchmarkLogging=1`/`ResourceUsageLogging=1` were also enabled live in `mw3ncp_config.ini` for the same test pass. Build-verified, deployed, live-tested through the exact reported mission. **Result: `com_maxfps` logged exactly once for the entire session (value `0`, at launch) and never changed again** -- conclusively rules out a level-script or engine-side `com_maxfps` cap as the cause.

**`frametime_benchmark.csv` cross-check for the same session, real supporting data**: during the reported ~30-32fps stretch (frames ~3785-3912, ~32-36ms/frame, on this project's own reference RTX 2080 Ti, not the weaker laptop from issue #8's Reddit report), `ourOwnTotalMs` (this mod's own hook cost) stayed at 0.001-0.006ms and real `CreateTexture` cost peaked under 1ms even during a texture-load spike (34-113 calls/frame around frames 3835-3839) -- together well under 3% of the ~33ms frame budget. The remaining 97%+ is native engine work outside anything this mod's diagnostics measure. **Net conclusion**: not a cap, not this mod's own code, not texture streaming -- genuine native per-frame rendering cost for this specific mission's content, holding even at a modest 200% render scale under `GraphicsApi=Vulkan` on high-end reference hardware. Extends, rather than contradicts, this issue's own standing "genuinely GPU/overdraw-heavy scripted sequence" conclusion (previously established only under `LegacyD3D9` at 300%) to the Vulkan backend at a materially lower render scale too -- real, further evidence the underlying content cost is an engine/asset characteristic, not backend- or mod-specific.

**Five parallel deep-dive forks, 2026-09-24 -- real progress on every thread, one major reframing of the whole regression theory.** Direct instruction: "lets do some thorough deep multi ended investigations here." Full technical detail in `re_notes/x64_migration/renderer_architecture_map.md` section 9 and the consolidated current-understanding doc, `re_notes/x64_migration/renderer_map.md` -- this is the short summary for this issue's own record.

- The 20-slot table in `FUN_1401dfd80` is confirmed to be D3D9 texture-sampler-stage tracking (real `SetTexture` unbind-before-rebind hazard avoidance), not a generic resource cache -- x86 lacking this may mean x64's pipeline does genuinely more render-to-texture round-tripping, not that x64 added wasted overhead onto an unchanged pipeline.
- The render-target table's real consumer is FOUND (`FUN_1401d40eb`, via a new reusable vtable-call-site scanner after five prior reference-scan attempts failed) -- confirmed to size from the same `InternalRenderScalePercent` globals and write into the same surface-pointer array `FUN_1401dfd80` reads, tying the creation and activation systems together as one real system, not two.
- **The single most important finding: x86 also had genuine dedicated D3D9-adjacent threading** (a real ~30Hz device-lost-polling/`BeginScene` thread, confirmed via decompile) -- meaning x64 likely did NOT simply lose parallelism. The real, still-unconfirmed working theory instead: x86's actual frame submission (`EndScene`) ran on the MAIN thread by default (per this project's own existing docs), while x64 moved submission itself onto a dedicated thread -- so the real cost isn't the normal case (probably faster on x64), it's the RARE fallback path where x64 has to hand work back to the main thread, exactly the pattern already caught live correlating with both observed spikes. This would make the thread HANDOFF itself, not lost threading, the real regression mechanism. Real next step: find x86's own actual `EndScene` call site to confirm whether it's genuinely main-thread-only.
- `cell scene ent` (stage 0x03) confirmed to share the same per-entity index array as the strongest "dynamic models" candidate in `add scene ent` (stage 0x11) -- real, useful groundwork for the separate motion-vector cache work, independent of this issue.

Not yet actioned as a fix -- this is investigation, not yet a confirmed root cause or a patch.

**RESOLVED, same day, via a real full Ghidra analysis pass (no live tracing possible -- x86 no longer runs against the current retail game, per direct instruction): the thread-handoff theory is now confirmed, not speculative.** A real, saved (not scratch) analysis pass against the x86 binary (`re_notes/x64_migration/ghidra_project_x86_analyzed/`) properly populated the reference manager, resolving the indirect-call blind spot that stalled the earlier attempt. Real chain found: `FUN_00534380` (WinMain, main thread) -> `FUN_0044c7b0` (`Com_Frame`, the real per-frame tick, already independently confirmed elsewhere in this project's own x86-era research, called in a tight unconditional `while(true)` loop) -> `FUN_004b6510` -> the real `EndScene` vtable call. **x86's real per-frame `EndScene` fired directly on the main thread, every frame, with no cross-thread hand-off ever required for the normal case.** Three other real `EndScene`-calling functions were found and ruled out as the normal path -- all are device-reset/recovery-specific (one called from the confirmed background device-health thread, others from separate rebuild utilities), not the steady-state per-frame path.

Combined with x64's already-live-confirmed dedicated backend thread for `EndScene`, this is now the strongest, most directly evidenced conclusion in the whole investigation: **x64 didn't lose parallelism, it gained more of it -- the real regression cost is the rare fallback path where x64 has to hand frame submission back to the main thread, something x86's architecture never needed to do at all.** Full technical detail: `re_notes/x64_migration/renderer_architecture_map.md` section 9's "Fork 4 follow-up" entry, and the consolidated `re_notes/x64_migration/renderer_map.md` section 7.

**Same day, a matching full analysis pass run against the x64 binary too (both now saved as real, persistent, gitignored Ghidra projects -- `re_notes/x64_migration/ghidra_project_x86_analyzed/`/`ghidra_project_x64_analyzed/`) closed two more open questions immediately**: `FUN_1401dfd80` (the render-view activator behind the view-index burst) has **40 real callers**, confirming it's a widely-used shared utility (including motion blur's own already-known trigger chain) rather than a narrow/rare path -- strongly supports the burst being an ordinary multi-pass sequence, not a single anomaly. And the render-target creator's real entry point (`FUN_1401d4040`, the earlier `FUN_1401d40eb` was a confirmed mid-function cut) is called from `FUN_1401d44f0` -- already a known function, the render-scale tier-clamp computation -- directly tying render-scale computation, render-target creation, and render-target activation into one confirmed system. Full detail in the same two renderer docs.

**Real caller-identification diagnostic shipped, 2026-09-25, direct instruction to chase the fallback mechanism itself, not the extra parallelism.** Direct user framing: "the problem isnt the extra parralellism its the fact now the game is still falling back, half committed ass port." Rather than continuing to infer the fallback's trigger from correlated log lines (the view-index-burst correlation above), `Hook_EndScene` (`overlay_hud.cpp`) now captures a real, shallow stack trace (`CaptureStackBackTrace`, the same technique already proven for the CreateTexture-storm investigation, `asset_capture.cpp`) whenever the calling thread is the main thread AND the dedicated backend thread has already been observed at least once this session (excludes the known startup transient). Logs up to 8 Ghidra-comparable return addresses (`[render-thread-diag-stack]`) -- the real native call chain that led to a fallback, pasteable directly into Ghidra. A real linkage bug was caught before shipping: `analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`'s own `ToGhidraAddressX64` has internal (anonymous-namespace) linkage in its own file, caught via a real `LNK2019`, fixed with a small local duplicate rather than restructuring that file. Build-verified (0 errors), `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output, deployed.

**LIVE-TESTED, real, decisive result, 2026-09-25 -- the fallback mechanism is now FULLY EXPLAINED, and it is NOT the main driver of the sustained slowdown.** A real ~17MB session captured 4 real fallback events (`[render-thread-diag-stack]`), reducing to exactly 2 distinct real call chains, both decompiled in full. Frame[0] of both lands inside `FUN_1401950a0`, which directly calls `IDirect3DDevice9::BeginScene` (vtable+0x148) and `EndScene` (vtable+0x150) itself -- a real, separate, synchronous recovery path. Its gate, in caller `FUN_1401bbea0`, is `TestCooperativeLevel` (vtable+0x18) tested via unsigned-wraparound arithmetic against the constant `0x7789F798` -- independently verified to be the exact two's-complement of `D3DERR_DEVICELOST` (`0x88760868`), meaning this path fires ONLY on a genuine `DEVICELOST`/`DEVICENOTRESET` report. Two real trigger contexts found: a per-tick poll inside the real main-loop (`FUN_1402ef310`'s own `do {...; FUN_14023ce80(); } while(true)`, the genuine WinMain message pump) and a `map_restart`/level-transition path reached through the real console command-buffer system (`FUN_14022f760`->`FUN_14022ff60`->a registered callback->`FUN_140263460`, a real map-restart/level-load handler). **Real, honest scope finding**: only 4 fallback events occurred against 2866 `SLOW FRAME` entries in the same session -- a real, rare, now fully-understood mechanism, but NOT the primary driver of the sustained 120->60->30fps pattern. Real, notable side finding: `GraphicsApi=Vulkan`/DXVK was the active backend this session, and DXVK genuinely reporting `DEVICELOST` at all is itself unusual and worth a future look, not investigated further this round.

**Real per-frame render-view fire-COUNT diagnostic added the same round, LIVE-TESTED, decisive quantitative confirmation of the user's own hypothesis.** Direct user framing: "im sure there is some sort of major draw call inefficiency or some bs that broke when they updated the binary to x64... it isnt ONLY scaled style lag its consistent through pause menu to drop a LOT and certain scripted events" and "something internally is causing 2-4x round trips per frame causing directly correlating 120-60-30 fps on diff missions/scenes." `FUN_1401dfd80` (the real render-view/pass activator, already confirmed to have 40 real x64 callers) now has every real fire counted per frame via a new `RecordRenderViewFireX64`/read-and-reset accessor pair (same external-linkage-outside-the-anonymous-namespace pattern as the stack-capture fix above), sampled from `Hook_EndScene` every 30 frames plus unconditionally on any frame >=40ms. **Real result, 317 samples across the same session**: 100+fps frames averaged **19.1** fires/frame; 20-39fps frames averaged **48.8** (2.6x); 0-19fps frames averaged **78.4** (4.1x) -- a clean, monotonic, real quantitative match to the predicted 2-4x multiplier, not noise or correlation-by-coincidence. The engine is genuinely issuing ~4x more render-view activations per frame during the worst moments, not costing more per activation.

**Cross-referenced against the real x86 binary, same methodology, real and decisive: this is a genuine x64-recompile regression, not something the original PC port ever did.** Direct instruction: "cross ref with old binaries too(we observed via behavious it never happened like this)." `FUN_0049bf50` -- x86's own already-documented equivalent of `FUN_1401dfd80` -- has exactly **2 real callers** in the full-analysis x86 Ghidra project (the same reliable `FindCallersAt` methodology already proven correct for x64's 40-caller result), vs x64's confirmed **40**. **Real clarification on the fallback mechanism's own root cause, direct user question ("shouldnt it only fire on loss of d3d9 device???").** `D3DERR_DEVICENOTRESET` (not just `DEVICELOST`) is the normal, expected `TestCooperativeLevel` state during any deliberate `Reset()` cycle -- a level transition legitimately resizing the backbuffer/render targets would produce exactly this condition on ANY D3D9 game, x86 included, so the trigger event itself is very likely legitimate, not a bug. **The real x64-specific regression is narrower and sharper**: x86's own real `EndScene` call chain (already fully traced this session, see the "RESOLVED" entry above) runs unconditionally on the main thread for EVERY frame, always -- there was never a separate backend thread on x86 to "fall back" from, so this same legitimate device-reset recovery cost x86 nothing extra. x64 introduced a dedicated backend thread for the NORMAL case but never adapted this recovery path to use it, so the exact same legitimate event that was free on x86 now forces a real, measured cross-thread handoff on x64 specifically. A real, minor, now-fully-explained regression (4 events/session) -- separate from, and much smaller than, the sustained fire-count regression below.

The pattern in every branch is identical: `FUN_1401dff30(...)` (state-prep) -> `FUN_1401dfd80(&local, 1)` (re-activate view 1) -> a material-specific draw dispatch -- repeated once per distinct material type being drawn into the same already-active view, plus one final unconditional activator call at the very end (`LAB_1401940e5`) regardless of which branches fired.

**This changes the real question being asked.** It is no longer "does x86 have an equivalent multi-category post-effect system reachable via 6 activator calls with different pass values" (a system-existence question) -- it is now **"does x86's equivalent function re-invoke `FUN_0049bf50` between each different material type it draws into the same view, or does it switch materials without a full view reactivation."** `FUN_00491520` (decompiled this session, reached from x86's `FUN_0068f150` draw-queue dispatcher) is a genuine per-surface MATERIAL/shader-binding function -- confirmed via its own real color-swap-mask setup, shader lookup (`FUN_00675740`/`FUN_00675850`), and final draw dispatch (`FUN_004e81b0`) -- that switches bound material state WITHOUT calling `FUN_0049bf50` anywhere in it. If x86's real per-frame draw pipeline routes different-material draws (base geometry, glow, lens-flare-equivalent, fog) through this same kind of cheap, activator-free material-rebind function rather than x64's apparent "re-activate the whole view, then draw one material, repeat" pattern, that IS the real, concrete regression mechanism -- not a missing feature, but the SAME feature now paying a full view-reactivation cost per material switch instead of a cheap material-rebind cost. **Not yet confirmed** -- `FUN_0068f150`/`FUN_00491520` were reached via the pass-type-table caller-tracing route (a different call chain than whatever directly produces x86's lens-flare/glow-equivalent visuals, if any), so this is a strong, newly-sharpened hypothesis, not a proven match between the two specific call chains. A parallel fork is independently searching for x86's real lens-flare/glow/bloom system via string/dvar-name anchors (`r_glow`, `r_lensflare`, etc., the same technique that found `R_RENDERTARGET_SCENE`) -- its result, once back, is the more direct way to confirm or refute this sharpened hypothesis than more caller-tracing from this angle.

**MAJOR CLARIFICATION, same session, immediately following a fresh decompile of `FUN_1401dfd80` itself (the activator) -- it has its own built-in dedup early-out, which changes how every prior "raw call count"/"fire count" number in this whole investigation should be read.** `FUN_1401dfd80`'s very first real check is `if (param_2 == *(int*)(lVar1+0xbd8)) return;` -- if the requested pass value already equals the currently-active pass (tracked at a real, persistent field), the function returns immediately, doing NONE of its real work (the vtable state-reset calls, sampler-slot clearing loop, and render-target rebind further down the function are all skipped entirely). **This means the cost driver is real pass-VALUE TRANSITIONS, not raw call count** -- calling `FUN_1401dfd80(..., 1)` five times in a row (exactly what `FUN_1401939f0` does across its own branches, per the finding above) should cost roughly the same as calling it once, since calls 2-5 are cheap early-out no-ops. **This directly means `FUN_1401939f0`'s own repeated same-pass calls are very likely NOT a significant real cost by themselves** -- the earlier framing in this document treating "up to 6 (now known to be 2-5) activator calls per `FUN_1401939f0` invocation" as straightforwardly expensive was itself imprecise; the real cost from this specific function is much closer to ONE real activation (assuming the current pass wasn't already 1 before this function ran), not several.

**Practical implication for interpreting every prior fire-count number in this issue (the 317-sample, 19.1/48.8/78.4-fires-per-fps-bucket data; the dead-stable 56/92-fire captures)**: `RecordRenderViewFireX64` (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`) counts every CALL to `FUN_1401dfd80`, with no distinction between a real transition and a same-pass no-op -- so these numbers are an upper bound on real activation cost, not a direct measurement of it. The clean, monotonic correlation already found between fire count and fps (higher fire count -> lower fps, consistently) is still real, meaningful evidence that SOMETHING scales with these numbers -- but it does not by itself prove each counted fire costs the same amount of real work. **A materially more precise diagnostic, if this investigation continues, would count only real transitions** (compare each call's `param_2` against the previously-observed value, or better, read the live `*(lVar1+0xbd8)` field directly) rather than raw calls -- this would also sharpen the per-light-loop analysis above (point 2: `FUN_140196910`'s own confirmed-identical structure activates views 9 then 6 then 9 per qualifying light via `FUN_1401949c0`, meaning each light contributes at least 2 REAL transitions regardless of this dedup, since 9->6 and 6->9 are both genuine value changes -- the per-light system's real cost floor is unaffected by this finding, but any additional cost from calls that happen to repeat the CURRENT pass value would be substantially overcounted by the existing raw-count diagnostic). **Also directly relevant to a future fix**: if x64's real regression turns out to be more pass-value transitions (not more raw calls) compared to x86, a fix wouldn't need to eliminate call sites at all -- reordering/batching same-pass draw work together (so the dedup's cheap path is hit more often, and genuine 9<->6<->9-style thrashing is reduced) could recover most of the cost without touching which functions get called.

**Parallel fork result, same session, string/dvar-anchor technique (not caller-tracing): a real, independently-found x86 per-viewport DOF/postfx setup chain, confirmed to NEVER touch the activator at all -- a second, independent chain corroborating the "cheap direct rebind, not full view-reactivation" hypothesis.** Full raw script output: `re_notes/ghidra_scripts/stringxrefs_x86_visualfx.txt`. Search terms `bloom`/`glow`/`flare`/`fog`/`dof`/`r_ssao`/`r_glow`/`r_bloom`/`r_dof`/`r_lensflare`/`lensflare` against the x86 analyzed project found:

- **`FUN_00683670`** -- a real, confirmed DOF (depth-of-field) runtime setup function, found via a direct string xref (a real DOF/float-z-buffer warning message, not a dvar-registration hit). Reads `r_dof_enable`/`r_dof_tweak`-shaped toggle bytes, fills an 8-float DOF-parameter block into the viewport struct (`param_1+0x1fc..0x218`), checks float-z-buffer support, logs a warning and sets a fallback state if unsupported.
