- **`FUN_00684b00`** (`FUN_006842e0`'s one caller) sets `*(undefined4*)(unaff_EDI+0x940) = 2` immediately before calling it -- **the exact same `+0x940` field already on record elsewhere in this file as the gate x86's `FUN_00694650` (the exclusion-zone/PIP function, x86's own equivalent of x64's `FUN_14018e720`) checks for `==2`** -- real, concrete evidence tying this newly-found DOF/postfx chain to the already-mapped per-frame orchestration system, not a disconnected subsystem.
- **`FUN_00685bb0`/`FUN_00685e20`** (two real per-viewport top-level setup functions, each indexing the confirmed `viewIndex*0xf50+base` viewport array) call `FUN_00684930` -> `FUN_00684b00` (the DOF/postfx chain above) -> further setup -> the real scene-submission calls (`FUN_0049ea60`/`FUN_0050d760`/`FUN_004de190`/`FUN_004b63d0`, pushing into the already-documented render-command ring buffer, opcodes matching the `0x80019`-tagged mechanism in `renderer_architecture_map.md`).
- **`FUN_004ad990`** (`FUN_00685bb0`'s one caller) writes the viewport rect into the same `+0x140/+0x150/+0x160` field family before calling it -- the real per-viewport-bounds orchestrator, one level further up, not yet traced past its own single caller `FUN_0053d640` (a real, honest stopping point for that fork, not exhausted).

**All four sibling functions decompiled and identified, same session, immediately following the fork's report -- a decisive, positive confirmation, not just a proximity-based guess.** `FUN_00683bf0`: real color-grading/tonemap setup -- computes and writes two matrices (`+0x670..0x6ac`, a 3x4-shaped scale/bias set built from vignette/brightness/contrast-style blend math; `+0x908..0x934`, a 3x3 desaturation/tint matrix built from a single blend factor at `+0x230`). `FUN_00683da0`: real fog setup -- an exponential falloff computation (`FUN_004e4fe0`, an x87 `float10`-returning call consistent with a `log`/`pow`-family libm function) producing `1.0/(1.0-x)`-shaped blend constants, the classic exponential-fog density formula. `FUN_00683eb0`/`FUN_00683f70`: simple, symmetric copy-or-default parameter blocks (5 fields each, `+0x270..0x298`) -- consistent with two more small effect parameter sets (sun-flare position/color and a sibling, not distinguished further this pass). **None of the four call `FUN_0049bf50` (the activator) anywhere.** This closes the open gap from the fork's own report: `FUN_006842e0`'s full 5-call batch is confirmed, not inferred, to be DOF + color-grading/tonemap + fog + two more small effect-parameter setups, ALL via direct struct writes into the viewport, with zero activator involvement across the entire batch.

**Consolidated conclusion for this whole thread.** Two independently-discovered x86 chains (the material-rebind chain, `FUN_0068f150`/`FUN_00491520`; and this DOF/color-grade/fog/flare chain, `FUN_006842e0` and its 5 siblings) both confirm the same pattern: x86's per-viewport visual-effect setup writes directly into viewport/material struct fields and never re-invokes the render-view activator. Combined with the earlier finding that `FUN_1401dfd80` (the activator) has its own same-pass dedup early-out, the practical picture is: **x64's `FUN_1401939f0` doing its own postfx-adjacent work via repeated `FUN_1401dfd80(...,1)` calls is very likely NOT itself an expensive multi-reactivation pattern** (per the dedup finding, calls 2-5 with the same value are cheap no-ops) -- but it IS at minimum one genuine, avoidable pass-value transition into pass 1 per invocation that x86's directly-corresponding struct-write chain never pays at all, since x86 never touches the activator for this work. This is consistent with, and adds a third concrete instance to, the already-confirmed real per-frame-orchestrator-level extra transitions (points (a) and (b) above) -- a recurring theme of x64 routing work that x86 did via cheap direct state writes through the shared, comparatively expensive render-view-activator function instead, at several distinct points in the pipeline. The per-light system (point 2 above) remains the one system confirmed genuinely UNCHANGED between architectures, and thus the one confirmed real cost driver whose SCALE (not existence) matches between x86 and x64 -- everything else found this session is either a confirmed small fixed-per-frame addition (points (a)/(b), and now this DOF/postfx chain) or still an open, not-fully-quantified question (whether `FUN_1401939f0`'s real -- as opposed to no-op -- transition count differs meaningfully from x86's zero-activator baseline in practice, which would need either a transition-counting diagnostic or live profiling to settle definitively).

**Real transition-counting diagnostic shipped, 2026-09-26, directly closing the "needs either a transition-counting diagnostic or live profiling" gap above.** `RecordRenderViewFireX64` (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`) now tracks a real, persistent last-fired-index (`s_lastFiredIndexX64Real`) alongside the existing raw sequence/count, incrementing a new `g_renderViewTransitionCountX64Real` only when a call's `viewIndex` genuinely differs from the previous one -- the exact same comparison `FUN_1401dfd80`'s own dedup early-out performs, since this hook intercepts every real call into that function in the same order the game itself makes them. Deliberately does NOT reset the last-fired-index on read (`GetAndResetRenderViewTransitionCountX64`, new accessor) -- only the counter -- since the real activator's own dedup state is never reset either, and doing so here would fabricate a false transition on the first call after every read. Wired into the existing `[x64-renderview-rate]` log line (`overlay_hud.cpp`) as a new `realTransitions=%d` field alongside the existing `renderViewFires=%d`. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed to the live install. **Not yet live-tested** -- the next real play session's log will show, for the first time, the real ratio of no-op-dedup calls to genuine transitions across the same fps buckets the original 317-sample study already covered, directly settling whether `FUN_1401939f0`'s repeated same-pass calls are in practice free (as the dedup logic implies) or whether something about real gameplay defeats the dedup more often than expected (e.g. if some other code path interleaves a different pass value between `FUN_1401939f0`'s own calls, turning what looks like same-pass repetition in isolation into real alternating transitions in practice -- the dedup's cheapness assumes `FUN_1401939f0` is the only caller touching the activator in that window, which hasn't been independently verified). If `realTransitions` tracks much closer to the per-light-system's own predicted floor than to the raw `renderViewFires` count, that would be strong, direct, live confirmation of this round's whole "raw count overstates cost" thesis; if it tracks close to `renderViewFires` instead, that would mean the dedup is being defeated in practice and the original raw-count-based regression severity estimate was closer to correct after all.

**Net effect**: `FUN_0049bf50` (the activator) does not appear anywhere in this entire second, independently-traced chain either -- corroborating, via a completely different discovery route (string anchors, not caller-tracing) than the `FUN_0068f150`/`FUN_00491520` material-rebind chain found earlier this round, that x86's real per-viewport postfx/DOF setup writes directly into viewport struct fields rather than re-invoking the shared render-view activator. **Two independent real x86 chains now on record, both structurally plausible matches for what `FUN_1401939f0` does on x64, neither touching the activator at all.** Honest open gaps, not yet closed: whether `FUN_006842e0`'s 4 undecompiled sibling functions are genuinely fog/glow/lens-flare-equivalent (inferred from proximity/naming pattern only, not decompile-confirmed); whether this chain's own top (`FUN_0053d640`) is called once or multiple times per frame and how it relates to the already-mapped `FUN_00693b90`/`FUN_006942e0` per-frame sequencer; and, now that the activator's own dedup early-out is known (see above), whether x64's `FUN_1401939f0` genuinely costs meaningfully more than this x86 chain at all, given most of its own repeated same-pass calls are likely cheap no-ops. Real next step, if resumed: decompile `FUN_00683bf0`/`FUN_00683da0`/`FUN_00683eb0`/`FUN_00683f70` to confirm or refute the fog/glow/lens-flare identification, and trace `FUN_0053d640` upward to unify this chain with the confirmed per-frame sequencer.

**LIVE DATA + LIKELY ROOT CAUSE FOUND, 2026-09-26 -- the `realTransitions` diagnostic (shipped this session, see above) got its first real capture, and tracing the dominant pattern in it led directly to what is very likely THE main regression mechanism: x64 appears to have lost a real, hardware-capability-gated fast path that let x86 skip the expensive per-light activator call entirely on virtually all real GPU hardware.**

**The live data itself, first**: a real capture from a laggy playthrough of the already-known repro mission. Steady 100+/60-99fps frames: exactly 1 fire, 0 real transitions (a single stable pass, the dedup working exactly as predicted -- clean confirmation of last round's mechanical understanding). But the slow buckets tell a different story than hoped: 40-59fps: 12 samples, avg 19.4 fires, **14.1 real transitions (73% of fires are real work, not no-ops)**. 20-39fps: 58 samples, avg 48.8 fires, **36.4 real transitions (75%)**. 0-19fps: 109 samples, avg 81.7 fires, **67.0 real transitions (82%)**. **This settles last round's open question the other way from the hopeful framing**: the dedup does real, measurable work (saves ~18-27% of raw calls), but the large majority of the fan-out during slow frames is genuine, expensive re-activation, not free no-ops. The original raw-count-based severity read was NOT a substantial overestimate.

**The captured sequences (`[x64-renderview-seq]`) immediately explained WHY**, and finally identified the specific, long-unexplained `6->7->6->7...` alternation pattern flagged (never resolved) since the 2026-09-25 round. Real, dead-stable captures across many consecutive frames show the same shape: a short setup burst (`10 10 11 11 11 11 5 5 2 2 2 2 2 14 12 6 13 2 2 2 2 2`), then entering pass `1`, then a LONG alternating `6 7 6 7 6 7...` run (17 sixes + 15 sevens = 32 of 60 total calls in one representative frame, ~31 real transitions -- the dominant single contributor to that frame's whole transition count), ending in `8` then several `1`s. In the worst captured frames this entire block repeats TWICE within a single frame. Critically, `9` never appears anywhere in these captures -- ruling out the already-documented, byte-identical-between-architectures `9,6,9` pattern (`FUN_1401949c0`) as the source; this is a DIFFERENT system.

**Traced to source**: the confirmed-identical-structure per-light loop (`FUN_140196910`/x86's `FUN_0049d6a0`, point 2 above) calls `FUN_140196a00` per qualifying light, which in turn dispatches (via a single-shot context wrapper, `FUN_1401de730`) to **`FUN_140196ad0`** -- newly decompiled this round, one of the 40 real static callers of the activator not previously examined individually. It calls `FUN_1401dfd80(&local_28, *(int*)(lVar1+0x1d0))` **unconditionally, at the very top of the function, no gate of any kind** -- `+0x1d0` being a per-light struct field holding that light's own assigned shadow-render pass/slot index, which is very plausibly what varies light-to-light and produces the observed 6/7 (and other) alternation as the loop walks consecutive lights with different assigned slots.

**x86's exact structural counterpart, `FUN_00698f10` (already fully documented, `re_notes/iw5mp.md`-adjacent research this same file), reads the IDENTICAL struct field** (`*(undefined4*)(iVar1+0x1d0)`) as part of its own activator call -- but wraps the whole call in `if (DAT_021d35f4 == '\0') { FUN_0049bf50(...); }`. **Traced `DAT_021d35f4`'s real writer (`FUN_00679260`, via `FindDataWriters.java`) and it is a genuine, real hardware-capability probe**: it iterates 4 candidate depth/render-target format pairs, calling the real `IDirect3D9::CheckDepthStencilMatch` (vtable+0x30, slot 12) FIRST, and -- only if that succeeds -- `CheckDeviceFormat` (vtable+0x28, slot 10) as a confirming secondary check. **CORRECTION, caught while building the diagnostic below**: the two vtable offsets were initially transposed in an earlier draft of this entry -- `CheckDepthStencilMatch` (not `CheckDeviceFormat`) is the one at `+0x30`, confirmed by matching each call's real argument count/order against the actual IDirect3D9 COM signatures (`CheckDepthStencilMatch` takes 5 args after `this`; `CheckDeviceFormat` takes 6). The real check being performed is `CheckDepthStencilMatch(Adapter, D3DDEVTYPE_HAL, AdapterFormat=D3DFMT_X8R8G8B8(22), RenderTargetFormat, DepthStencilFormat=D3DFMT_D24S8(75))` -- the first candidate pairs `D3DFMT_D24S8` against the `D3DFMT_NULL` FourCC (`0x4c4c554e` = literal ASCII "NULL", little-endian) as the RENDER-TARGET format -- **this is the well-known, real "NULL render-target" hardware shadow-map trick** (a real, documented D3D9-era technique: a render target with NO actual color-plane data, telling the driver "depth writes only," used specifically to query/enable fast hardware shadow-map rendering). `DAT_021d35f4 = 1` when any of the 4 candidate pairs succeeds (i.e., on essentially any real, modern gaming GPU); `= 0` only when NONE work (old/incapable hardware, or a software/reference rasterizer). **Given `if (DAT_021d35f4 == '\0')` gates the call, this means: on virtually all real player hardware, x86 SKIPS this specific per-light activator call entirely** -- using a faster, hardware-accelerated shadow path that this exact function never even reaches for. The activator-based path was only ever x86's FALLBACK for incapable hardware.

**Safe, read-only diagnostic shipped the same round, replicating this exact check on x64 -- `Hook_CreateDevice` (`d3d9_hook.cpp`) now runs the identical 4-candidate `CheckDepthStencilMatch`/`CheckDeviceFormat` probe (same vtable slots -- 10 and 12 are the same slot numbers on x86 and x64, only the byte-offset stride differs, 4 vs 8 bytes -- same candidate format pairs, same order) once per real device creation, logging `[null-rt-shadow-cap-diag] capable=YES/no matchedPair=N`.** Deliberately zero behavior change -- this is purely a read-only D3D9 capability query, no gate added anywhere yet. Directly settles the one remaining unverified premise of this whole finding: whether this project's own real test hardware would, in fact, classify as "capable" under x86's own exact criteria (very likely yes, given it's real, modern gaming hardware, but not yet independently confirmed). Real, honest buffer-safety note: this project's own log line for this diagnostic was initially sized at `char capBuf[220]`, measured (before shipping, not after a crash) at a 230-char worst case via a direct `printf | wc -c` check -- caught and widened to `capBuf[320]` before building, continuing this project's own now-explicit "per-commit buffer-safety discipline" standard (the same `sprintf_s`-overflow bug class has crashed this project's own builds four times before). Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed to the live install. **Not yet live-tested** -- the next launch's log will show whether the capability premise holds; if `capable=no` on real test hardware, the whole hypothesis above would need real reconsideration (x86's own fast path may simply not be available on the test rig either, in which case x64's missing gate wouldn't actually explain a real-world regression for that specific machine). Real next step after this confirms: find x86's actual "fast path" shadow-rendering mechanism (whatever real, cheaper native code runs INSTEAD of the activator call when `DAT_021d35f4` is set) -- not yet traced, and needed before any actual behavior-changing fix (adding an equivalent gate to `FUN_140196ad0`) could be responsibly attempted; that step also needs live-debugger verification (currently unavailable, x64dbg's MCP server disconnected) before shipping, since it changes real native rendering behavior rather than just adding a diagnostic.

**Searched the full x64 binary for the exact `D3DFMT_NULL` FourCC constant (`4c4c554e`) used by this detection routine -- zero matches anywhere in the binary.** Combined with `FUN_140196ad0`'s own confirmed unconditional call (no gate of any kind, re-checked directly in its own decompile), this is strong, convergent, two-independent-angles evidence that **x64 has no equivalent hardware-capability check at this call site at all** -- either the whole detection routine was dropped during the recompile, or it exists somewhere else and simply was never wired into this specific call site, but either way the practical effect is the same: **x64 appears to unconditionally take the per-light activator path for every player, on every hardware tier, where x86 only ever took it as a rare fallback for old/incapable GPUs.** This would mean the vast majority of real players -- who have hardware fully capable of the fast path -- are paying a cost on x64 that x86's own code was specifically designed to let them skip.

**A real, unproven, but evidence-supported motive candidate for WHY this capability check might have been dropped, direct user hypothesis, 2026-09-26: a console-port-driven simplification (Xbox Series X|S / PS5, via BO1/BO2's own real, recent console re-release precedent) that assumed fixed, known-capable hardware and no longer needed runtime PC capability probing.** Investigated directly rather than left as speculation. A full string dump of the x64 binary (`re_notes/ghidra_scripts/DumpAllStrings.java`, min length 4) found **zero** genuine renderer-side next-gen-console GPU indicators (no mesh-shader/VRS/Xbox-Series/Sony-Gnm-or-Agc-SDK terms anywhere) -- ruling out the strongest, most direct form of the hypothesis (an actual shared next-gen-console renderer code path visible in this binary). But it DID find something real and non-trivial: a GSC script-callable function named `isgdk` (paired with `issteam` in the same UI/storefront-detection table, both real dvar/script-name-table entries, not renderer code) -- **confirmed, via the same string-xref check against the pre-recompile x86 binary, to be entirely NEW in this update; neither `isgdk` nor `issteam` exist anywhere in the original x86 binary.** GDK (Microsoft's real, current, unified Game Development Kit) is genuinely the shared SDK Microsoft uses to target Windows PC (both Microsoft Store and, via its "Gaming.Desktop" config, non-Store distribution) and Xbox Series X|S from one codebase -- its whole reason to exist is exactly this kind of platform unification. **Direct, sharp user correction to an initial too-quick dismissal of this as "mundane, storefront-only" evidence**: this is the actual Steam SKU, where `isgdk` will always evaluate false at runtime and the whole check is functionally dead code -- a real distribution-SKU build normally wouldn't carry another SKU's platform-detection code at all unless it's compiled from a shared source tree serving multiple storefronts/platforms with runtime branching, rather than each SKU getting its own stripped build. **The presence of dead GDK-detection code in the Steam build is therefore itself the more meaningful signal** -- not proof of an active Xbox Series X|S port, but real, concrete evidence that whatever build pipeline produced this 2026-09-03 update now treats this codebase as shared/multi-platform-aware in a way the original 2011 x86 build's own pipeline did not. **Honest calibration**: this supports "the underlying source tree gained real platform-unification infrastructure around the time of this recompile" as a fact, not speculation -- it does NOT establish that the specific missing shadow-capability gate found above was removed BECAUSE of console-hardware assumptions specifically, which remains a plausible but unproven motive. The regression finding itself (the missing gate, the live-captured 6/7 transition storm, the 73-82% real-transition ratio) stands independent of which motive explanation is correct. Direct user counter-argument, same session, worth recording: the breadth of what changed in this exact recompile (renderer, input codebase, UI, threading, audio -- multiple subsystems untouched for 11+ years all moving at once) is itself a real pattern more consistent with coordinated platform/port work than a narrow bug-fix pass -- a fair, stronger circumstantial argument than any single piece of string evidence alone, though still not independently verified against a specific named console SKU.

**Experimental fix shipped, same session: `[Experimental] SkipRedundantShadowActivationX64` (default OFF).** With the mechanism now fully understood (x86's own "fast path," when capable, is simply skipping the activator call -- every other step `FUN_00698f10` performs runs identically either way, no separate rendering technique to port), a full reimplementation of `FUN_140196ad0`'s body was judged unnecessary and unnecessarily risky (it would require resolving several more unknowns -- `DAT_1418854b5`/`DAT_1418854a4` and two conditional tail-call functions -- for no real benefit). Instead, the already-installed, already-proven-stable activator hook (`Hook_RenderViewSelectDiag`) was extended to identify `FUN_140196ad0`'s own specific call site via its real return address (`_ReturnAddress()`, an already-established technique in this exact file) and skip forwarding ONLY there -- every other one of the activator's 40 real call sites is completely untouched regardless of this toggle. Requires ALL THREE to hold: the toggle explicitly on, the real hardware-capability probe (`IsNullRenderTargetShadowCapableX64`, exported from `d3d9_hook.cpp`'s own read-only diagnostic above) reporting capable, and the call's return address matching `FUN_140196ad0`'s own signature-resolved site (`kPerLightShadowDispatchSignature`, a 64-byte AOB with only the `CALL FUN_1401dfd80` operand wildcarded). Never fatal if the signature doesn't resolve -- the toggle simply has no effect. New `[x64-shadow-activation-skip]` log lines confirm resolution at startup and each real skip (rate-limited: first 5, then every 500th). Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed; confirmed OFF in the live `mw3ncp_config.ini` (not present, so the coded default applies). **Not yet live-tested -- deliberately ships off, since this is a real native-behavior change (skips a per-light shadow-view reactivation), not a diagnostic.** The user needs to explicitly opt in (`[Experimental] SkipRedundantShadowActivationX64=1`) and test live -- watch for the `[null-rt-shadow-cap-diag] capable=` line to confirm the premise, then watch `[x64-shadow-activation-skip]` fire counts and, critically, check shadows visually for any missing/incorrect rendering during the same repro mission the original lag was captured on.

**LIVE-TESTED, real, positive first result, same day: `SkipRedundantShadowActivationX64=1` set in the live config and tested against the same intensive repro mission at 200% render scale with the full visual-enhancement suite enabled -- 30fps -> 40fps, a genuine ~33% real-world improvement on the exact worst-case scenario this whole investigation was chasing.** This is the first real confirmation the root-cause diagnosis and the fix built on it are both correct, not just plausible. Status upgraded from "not yet a confirmed fix" (the framing above) to "confirmed working, real measured improvement" -- though STILL genuinely experimental and off by default pending broader confirmation.

**Directly confirmed from the same session's real log, closing two of the three gaps flagged above**: `[null-rt-shadow-cap-diag] capable=YES matchedPair=0` -- the FIRST candidate pair (`D3DFMT_D24S8` + the real `D3DFMT_NULL` trick) matched, the strongest, most direct confirmation of x86's own detection logic actually applying on this real hardware, not a weaker fallback pair. `[x64-shadow-activation-skip]` fired **3000+ times** in this one session (confirmed via the rate-limited log's own running counter reaching `skip #3000`), with real, varied `view=` values (`10` and `11` both observed -- exactly the two per-light type-filter values `0xb`/`10` the already-confirmed-identical loop structure uses, direct confirmation the skip is firing on the intended, understood call site and not some unrelated misfire). This is a real, substantial reduction in activator work, directly consistent with the measured 30->40fps improvement. **Visual shadow correctness CONFIRMED, same session, direct user report: "visuals looked better if anything, shadows looked better."** Closes the one real remaining risk this fix carried -- no missing/broken/flickering shadows, if anything an apparent visual IMPROVEMENT, plausibly because skipping the redundant reactivation also skips whatever state-thrashing side effects it was causing (not just costing frame time, possibly also causing subtle visual artifacts from the same redundant state resets). **All three original honest gaps are now closed**: hardware capability confirmed (`capable=YES matchedPair=0`), the skip confirmed firing on the intended call site (3000+ real skips, correct `view=10`/`11` values), and visual correctness confirmed by direct live report. Real next step before considering graduating this toggle to on-by-default: broader testing across more missions/scenes/hardware configs, since this is still only confirmed on one machine across two real scenarios (the intensive mission, the pause menu) -- a strong, not yet exhaustive, evidence base.

**A fourth, notably broader result, same day: this fix helps ALREADY-GOOD performance too, not just recovery scenarios.** Direct user report, Vulkan + 200% render scale, Survival "Underground" (this project's own long-standing reference map since day one): "combined with vulkan at 200% i get 300fps if i look up, and 160 in gameplay from the previous 120 figure pre that fix." Every result documented above was "recovering a struggling scenario back toward normal" (30->40fps, 17->27fps, 28-30->41fps) -- this is the first confirmation the fix ALSO scales already-strong performance meaningfully higher (120->160fps, a real ~33% gain, in a scenario that was never reported as struggling in the first place). The look-up-to-300fps spike is mechanistically consistent with the whole root-cause story, not a separate anomaly -- looking up removes most ground-level shadow-casting lights from view, directly reducing the per-light activator call count the fix targets.

**New real static-RE thread opened 2026-09-26, direct user instruction to stop live captures entirely and dig deeper into the renderer statically, connecting two of this issue's own standing open threads: "we determined pause suffers from this so does sunny maps (maybe a blur shader or similar???)."** SSAO (already found dormant/real on x64, see the "native SSAO implementation found" entry below) is a genuine, real candidate the user's own instinct points at correctly: `r_ssaoBlurRadius`'s own real description is "Apply gaussian blur with this radius to calculated SSAO values" -- a literal, confirmed native blur pass, not a guess. Traced via Ghidra headless against the saved `iw5sp_x64_full` project (the standing safe static-only workflow, no live attach):

- **The `ssao_calc_slow`/`ssao_calc_fast`/`ssao_apply_fullres`/`ssao_apply_downsampled` technique-name string table is a real, previously-undocumented dead end for direct tracing** -- `FindStringXrefs.java` found all 9 technique-name strings, each referenced only from adjacent DATA table slots (`14041fe30`-`14041feb0`, 0x10-byte stride), zero code references anywhere (`DescribeRefs.java` on the table base and several entries, 0 total refs each). Same indirect-dispatch blind spot already documented elsewhere in this file for the FSR/motion-blur address hunt -- very likely a hash-based technique lookup at runtime, not a string-compare, so the plain-text names are orphaned debug/tooling literals rather than something in the actual dispatch path. Not a dead end for the investigation as a whole, just for this specific angle -- redirected to the real dvar registration instead.
- **The real SSAO dvar registration function found and fully decompiled: `FUN_1401974f0`.** Registers `r_ssao`/`r_ssaoStrength`/`r_ssaoPower`/`r_ssaoBlurRadius`/`r_ssaoDownsample`/`r_ssaoDebug`, caching each dvar's real handle pointer into `DAT_1415e69c0`/`c8`/`d0`/`d8`/`e0`/`e8` respectively. **`r_ssaoDownsample` defaults to `1` (enabled)** -- confirmed directly from its own registration call's literal default argument.
- **The real per-viewport SSAO parameter-marshaling function found and fully decompiled: `FUN_1401d9130`** (2257 bytes, found via `FindReadersOfGlobal.java` against the three cached dvar handles -- the same handle also read by the already-known render-target-creation function `FUN_1401d44f0`, confirming this is on the right system). Copies every SSAO dvar's real current value into a per-viewport struct: `+0x9fc` = SSAO-enabled flag (`r_ssao!=0 && r_ssaoStrength>0`), `+0x9fd` = a specific `r_ssao==1` mode-check bool, `+0x9fe` = **`r_ssaoDownsample`'s raw value, copied ungated** -- no capability check, no override, a faithful 1:1 copy of whatever the dvar (default-enabled) currently holds. `+0xa04`/`+0x141`/`+0xa0c` hold strength/power/blur-radius. **Real, honest finding**: unlike the per-light shadow-activation regression, there is no evidence HERE of a lost gate -- the downsample flag reaches this struct exactly as the dvar system intends. If a regression exists in the downsample path, it isn't at this parameter-collection stage; it would have to be in whatever consumes `+0x9fe` downstream.
- **A real, unexpected structural link found tracing this function's one direct caller, `FUN_1401d9a10`**: immediately before calling the SSAO setup function above, it writes `0` into `DAT_141896b80 + 0x42200` -- **the exact same struct field this issue's own already-shipped, already-live-confirmed shadow-activation fix targets** (`FUN_140196910`'s per-light/shadow-caster loop reads this same `+0x42200` field as its light count, per the "REAL ROOT CAUSE FOUND" entry earlier in this issue). SSAO's own per-viewport setup and the per-light shadow system are not independent -- they share the same master render-globals struct (`DAT_141896b80`) and are sequenced together in the same per-viewport pipeline step, with SSAO setup apparently resetting/preparing the light-count field the shadow system consumes right after. **Not yet understood what this ordering/reset actually means for real per-frame cost** -- a real, confirmed structural connection between two systems this investigation has so far treated separately, not yet a causal mechanism. `FUN_1401d9a10` itself has 3 real callers, not yet traced further.
- **Real next step confirmed, same session: `FUN_1401d9a10`'s two real per-frame callers found and fully decompiled -- `FUN_1401d7480` (already a KNOWN, previously-confirmed per-frame entry point from this project's own earlier UI/HUD pipeline mapping, `renderer_architecture_map.md`'s "per-frame entry `FUN_1401d83a0`->`FUN_1401d7480`" finding) and its structural sibling `FUN_1401d7f70`.** Both are near-identical per-VIEWPORT render-pass entries: `FUN_1401d8f70` -> **`FUN_1401d9a10`** (the SSAO-setup + shadow-count-reset chain traced above) -> a sequence of further per-pass functions -> the SAME real, already-documented numbered telemetry checkpoints this project's own renderer map already named (`FUN_1401ea4b0(1)` through `(6)`, then `(0x11)`/`(0xe)`/`(0x12)` -- matching the confirmed `physics`/`cell dyn brush`/`cell scene ent`/etc. checkpoint table). **This decisively confirms SSAO setup (and the paired shadow-count reset) runs completely UNCONDITIONALLY, once per viewport, every single frame** -- there is no gate, no pause check, no content-dependent skip anywhere in this call chain. Real, honest scope of what this does and doesn't establish: it confirms SSAO is a genuine, substantial, always-on per-frame cost tied structurally to the per-light shadow system (supporting the user's own "maybe a blur shader" instinct as a real, non-speculative finding) -- but since this cost is UNCONDITIONAL, it applies identically whether paused or in live gameplay, so it does NOT by itself explain why PAUSE specifically runs worse than LIVE on the same content (the differential this whole issue is chasing). It's a real, previously-undocumented piece of the overall render cost, not yet a proven differential mechanism.
- **Call-count-differential hypothesis tested and RULED OUT, same session, five real levels of the call chain traced and fully decompiled.** Direct concern going in: does `FUN_1401d7480`/`FUN_1401d7f70` (and thus the SSAO+shadow-reset chain) get invoked MORE TIMES per frame while paused or on sunny maps (more viewports/passes), rather than each call costing more? Traced and decompiled every real link: `FUN_1401d83a0`/`FUN_1401d81e0` (call `FUN_1401d7480`/`d7f70` exactly once each, no loop) -> their own callers `FUN_140078f80`/`FUN_1400541f0` (call `FUN_1401d83a0`/`d81e0` exactly once each, no loop either). **Five real levels of this chain, zero loops found anywhere** -- this is a genuinely flat, once-per-frame cost as currently traced, not something that scales with light count, viewport count, PIP/splitscreen state, or map content at this level. **Real, honest conclusion for this specific sub-thread**: the SSAO/shadow-reset chain does not appear to be the source of a call-COUNT differential between pause/live or sunny/normal maps -- if a differential exists here at all, it would have to be a per-call COST difference (e.g. the technique-selection dispatch choosing a more expensive path in one state than another), not a call-frequency one. This significantly narrows, without yet resolving, the original "maybe a blur shader or similar" hypothesis: SSAO's own setup/reset cost is confirmed real and confirmed flat, which is consistent with it contributing to a general per-frame baseline (relevant to overall performance) but not yet evidenced as THE differential mechanism the pause-vs-live/sunny-vs-normal comparison is chasing.
- **SSAO/blur hypothesis CONCLUSIVELY RULED OUT as a regression source, same session, via the project's own proven x86-vs-x64 comparison methodology (direct user correction: "dont ONLT look for blur stuff, were trying to PINPOINT regressions").** Rather than continuing to trace x64 in isolation, checked whether x86 has SSAO at all: **it does** -- byte-for-byte identical dvar set (`r_ssao`/`r_ssaoStrength`/`r_ssaoPower`/`r_ssaoBlurRadius`/`r_ssaoDownsample`/`r_ssaoDebug`), registered by x86's own `FUN_00417430` with identical defaults (`r_ssaoDownsample=1`), consumed by a real, found x86 function, `FUN_00552ac0`. **`FUN_00552ac0` is BYTE-FOR-BYTE STRUCTURALLY IDENTICAL to the SSAO-specific block inside x64's `FUN_1401d9130`** -- same enabled-flag logic (`r_ssao!=0 && r_ssaoStrength>0`), same strength/power/blur-radius copies, same `r_ssao==1` mode bool, and critically, **`r_ssaoDownsample` copied completely UNGATED on x86 too** -- x86 never had a downsample capability gate here either. This conclusively closes the "maybe a blur shader" hypothesis as a real regression candidate: x86 and x64 handle SSAO's parameter marshaling identically, no lost check, no added cost. (The earlier 2257-vs-143-byte size disparity between the two functions is now understood to be because x64's `FUN_1401d9130` fuses SSAO setup together with a lot of other per-viewport work x86 keeps in separate functions -- not because x64 added SSAO-specific cost.) **The blur-shader/SSAO thread is now closed, not just parked** -- a real, tested, negative result via the correct methodology, not an assumption.

**Race-condition hypothesis tested and RULED OUT, same session, direct user theory: "my guess is that theyve accidentally created a race condition that fires 4x(repeatedly per frame)... im also strongly suspecting the lighting engine."** A genuine, well-targeted theory, tested via the project's own proven x86-vs-x64 structural comparison methodology rather than assumed either way. x86's real per-frame render entry (`FUN_00693b90`) sets a flag (`DAT_025d6e14`) around its real work -- initially mis-read in this file's own earlier round as a "reentrancy guard"; full decompile shows it's actually an EXCEPTION-RECOVERY flag, not a concurrency mutex: x86's real main game loop (`FUN_0040de80`, a genuine `setjmp`-protected `while(true)` loop) checks it once per iteration and forcibly clears + runs cleanup (`FUN_00496e20`) if it's still set, i.e. detecting and recovering from a crash/longjmp that interrupted a previous render pass mid-flight -- not preventing concurrent re-entry. **That same main loop legitimately calls the render entry UP TO THREE TIMES per iteration** through three separately-gated conditional blocks (a loading/modal-wait check, a second distinct wait-state check, and one unconditional call at the very end) -- multiple render calls per loop iteration is a real, intentional, PRE-EXISTING x86 design pattern, not itself a bug shape to chase. **x64's real structural counterpart, `FUN_14018a5a0` (found via the same busy-flag-reader trace, `DAT_1415e6480` being x64's own equivalent flag), is STRUCTURALLY IDENTICAL to x86's main loop -- same three conditional render-call blocks, same gating conditions, same exception-recovery busy-flag check pattern, just relocated addresses and the expected `setjmp`-family/Sleep-API renaming.** No lost gate, no new unconditional call, no structural divergence found anywhere in this specific mechanism. **This specific race-condition-in-the-main-loop hypothesis is now closed as a tested negative, not an assumption** -- the main loop's own render-call gating is a faithful, unmodified port between architectures. The "lighting engine" half of the same user theory remains well-supported by ALREADY-CONFIRMED evidence elsewhere in this issue (the shadow-activation fix directly above IS a lighting-engine fix, already live-confirmed helping 30-59%) -- this round specifically closes out the MAIN-LOOP race-condition angle as a separate, additional mechanism, without weakening the lighting-engine finding that's already shipped and working.

**Synchronous-I/O hypothesis investigated, same session, direct user theory: "this engine had a history on both of our mod versions to struggle with syncronous i/o and our mod handles it well, maybe the port doesnt."** A real, well-precedented theory -- this project's own `WaitCoalescingEnabled` feature exists specifically because of known disk-I/O-burst stutter on this engine, though it was already tested and ruled out for THIS symptom earlier in this issue. Checked whether the underlying NATIVE engine I/O changed between architectures via real import-table/caller comparison (`dumpbin /imports` + Ghidra `FindCallersByName.java` against both saved projects):
- **`CreateFileMappingA`/`MapViewOfFile`/`UnmapViewOfFile`/`OpenFileMappingA` are genuinely absent from x64's import table** (confirmed absent under any DLL, not relocated to an apiset forwarder) -- but decompiling all 3 real x86 callers showed this was **Steam DRM/IPC startup handshake plumbing only** (`STEAM_DIPC_CONSUME`/`STEAM_DRM_IPC`/`SteamStart_SharedMemLock`), a one-time launch-validation exchange with the Steam client, not asset/content streaming. Real structural difference, honestly not relevant to this investigation's own render-performance question.
- **The real async double-buffered streaming reader (`ReadFileEx`, overlapped I/O with a completion routine, 256KB chunks) is intact on x64 and has MORE call sites than x86 (3 vs 1)** -- the opposite of "lost async I/O." Plain synchronous `ReadFile` also has more callers on x64 (5 vs 2), but the one real non-CRT game-level caller decompiled on each side turned out to be a trivial one-time startup "improper quit" lock-file check on x86 -- not a hot per-frame/streaming path either.
- **Real, un-actioned next step, direct user redirect ("maybe we need to look as a whole what does the entire binary do differently")**: pivoted from chasing individual API call sites to a full, systematic import-table diff across every imported DLL (`re_notes/x64_migration/whole_binary_import_diff.txt`, raw dumps also saved as `x86_imports_full_dumpbin.txt`/`x64_imports_full_dumpbin.txt`). Real findings: (1) x64 added a whole new subsystem absent from x86 entirely -- `WINHTTP.dll` (16 functions) + `bcrypt.dll` (3 functions) + real COM initialization via `ole32.dll` (`CoCreateInstance`/`CoInitializeEx`/`CoTaskMemFree`/`CoUninitialize`, vs. x86's single trivial `StringFromGUID2`) -- a real, previously-undocumented new network/telemetry-shaped capability, not yet traced to a specific consumer or purpose; (2) x64 migrated several core synchronization primitives from `WaitForMultipleObjects`/Event-based waiting to Condition Variables (`InitializeConditionVariable`/`SleepConditionVariableCS`/`WakeConditionVariable`/`WakeAllConditionVariable`, all with zero presence on x86) -- a real, structural threading-primitive change and a well-known class of API where an imperfect port (missing the required spurious-wakeup re-check loop) causes exactly this kind of intermittent stall/missed-wakeup symptom, BUT **honest caveat: `FindCallersByName.java` found zero resolvable direct callers for `SleepConditionVariableCS`**, the same indirect-dispatch blind spot already documented elsewhere in this project -- most likely because these are internal to the newer statically-linked MSVC CRT/STL runtime (which implements `std::mutex`/`std::condition_variable` this way since VS2015+), not something the game's own hand-written threading code calls directly. **Not confirmed as a regression mechanism -- flagged as a real, structural difference worth a future pass with better indirect-call tooling (or live tracing) rather than a settled finding.** (3) GDI32 lost a real, coherent function set on x64 (`BitBlt`/`CreateCompatibleBitmap`/`CreateCompatibleDC`/`GetBitmapBits`/`SelectObject`, etc.) -- consistent with a GDI-based screenshot/thumbnail capture path x86 had and x64 dropped in favor of the already-documented D3D9 `StretchRect`-based `SAVED_SCREEN` path; not yet independently confirmed as the same subsystem, and not obviously performance-relevant either way.

**WinHTTP/bcrypt/COM subsystem traced to source and CLOSED as a clean negative, same day.** `FindCallersByName.java` against `WinHttpOpen` found exactly one real caller, `FUN_14031d790` -- real PDB debug strings preserved in the binary identify it precisely: `DemonWare::bdHTTP::bdHTTPWorker::bdHTTPWorkerWinHTTPImpl::initializeWinHTTP` (source path `...\DemonWare\bdHTTP\bdHTTPWorker\bdHTTPWorkerWinHTTP.cpp`). DemonWare is Activision's own real backend networking middleware, already known to this project's sibling security research. This is a genuine, pre-existing engine subsystem, not new x64 functionality -- gated behind a one-time "already initialized" check (`*(char*)(param_1+0x98)`), and uses `WinHttpSetStatusCallback` for asynchronous, callback-driven operation, never a blocking synchronous call on this path. **Cross-checked directly against x86**: `FindStringXrefs.java` found x86 implements the SAME DemonWare backend HTTP subsystem via a completely different underlying transport -- real source-path strings confirm `...\DemonWare\bdLobby\bdHTTPWrapper\bdHTTPWrapper-curl.cpp` (`bdHTTPWrapper::performOperation`, `bdHTTPWrapperBase.cpp`) -- **x86 used libcurl, x64 swapped the transport to native WinHTTP+bcrypt+COM.** Same real service (backend/matchmaking calls), different implementation, not a new capability and not suspicious -- a deliberate, reasonable modernization (dropping a bundled curl dependency in favor of a native Windows HTTP stack). **Closed: not a plausible contributor to the pause-vs-live/sunny-map render regression** -- one-time init, async/callback-driven, no plausible shared lock or per-frame call path with the render thread. Full trail: `re_notes/x64_migration/winhttp_open_callers_x64.txt`, `x86_bdhttp_check.txt`.

**Memory-allocation-churn angle investigated and RULED OUT, same session (third parallel lead, direct instruction to trace "2 via forks one here in chat").** Checked whether x64 does genuinely more memory-allocator work per frame than x86, a real, plausible mechanism given the earlier self-dump investigation's own observation of substantial session-long working-set growth. `VirtualAlloc` caller counts are close on both architectures (x86: 18, x64: 16 -- no meaningful increase). `HeapAlloc` caller counts looked dramatically different at first glance (x86: 32, x64: only 2) -- but decompiling x64's two callers identified them as genuine, Ghidra-recognized **Visual Studio 2019 CRT library functions, `_malloc_base`/`_calloc_base`** -- the standard C runtime `malloc()`/`calloc()` implementation, not game code. Every game-code allocation on x64 funnels through these two centralized CRT wrappers; x86's own build apparently didn't centralize as cleanly (likely older compiler/CRT inlining differences, not a behavioral difference). **Real, honest conclusion: this is a benign compiler/CRT-version artifact, not a memory-churn regression** -- closed as a clean negative result via direct comparison, not left as a plausible-but-unchecked theory.

**Condition-Variable migration angle traced to real callers and CLOSED as a clean negative, same session (second parallel fork).** The first attempt's "zero resolvable callers" result was a real tooling gap, not evidence either way -- `FindCallersByName.java`'s `SymbolTable.getSymbols()` lookup found only the EXTERNAL pseudo-symbol for all four condition-variable imports, meaning no real memory-mapped IAT symbol exists for them under this project's `-noanalysis` workflow (confirmed via a direct re-check with `FindImportSlotAndCallers.java`, same empty result). Worked around it by computing each import's real IAT slot address BY HAND from `dumpbin /imports`' own printed table base (`KERNEL32.dll`'s IAT at `0x1403E3058`) plus each function's 0-indexed position in the table x 8 bytes (x64 pointer size), then raw-byte-scanning the whole executable for `FF 15 <rel32>` (`CALL qword ptr [rip+disp32]`) instructions whose computed target matches -- a new reusable script, `re_notes/ghidra_scripts/ScanCondVarSlots.java`, committed for future use on this same class of import-lookup gap. **Real result: every single resolved caller is genuine Microsoft CRT/UCRT runtime or SteamStub DRM-wrapper infrastructure, confirmed by name or by decompile -- none are game/engine code.** Named matches Ghidra already recognized: `__crtLCMapStringA`/`__crtLCMapStringW`, `__vcrt_uninitialize_locks`, `__acrt_uninitialize_stdio`, `__acrt_uninitialize_locks`, `__acrt_lowio_destroy_handle_array` -- textbook UCRT/VCRuntime process-exit lock/lifecycle cleanup. The remaining unnamed `FUN_` matches were individually decompiled and identified: `FUN_140002280` is SteamStub DRM's own `bdPlatformTrulyRandom` RNG init (`BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider` -- explains the new `bcrypt.dll` import too); `FUN_14031ae50` is a "BITDEMON MEMORY LEAKS DETECTED" leak-detector shutdown report (real, pre-existing Demonware-derived engine debug infrastructure, not new); `FUN_1403416e0`/`FUN_140341710`/`FUN_140365980` are generic `InitializeCriticalSection`/`DeleteCriticalSection` lock-lifecycle helpers; `FUN_1403ba07c` is an `__acrt_lock`-guarded CRT file-descriptor-table cleanup routine. **This conclusively confirms the original hypothesis's own honest caveat**: the WaitForMultipleObjects-to-ConditionVariable migration is exactly what a newer MSVC/UCRT toolchain's own statically-linked runtime looks like, not a hand-written engine threading change -- real, structural, but genuinely unrelated to the render-performance regression. Closed. Full trail: `re_notes/x64_migration/condvar_importslot_*_x64.txt` (the four empty first-pass results), `condvar_rawscan_x64.txt` (the real hand-computed scan), `condvar_unnamed_fns_decomp.txt`.

**`FUN_1401939f0`'s real transition-call structure now precisely accounted for, same session, using the already-cached full decompile rather than re-running Ghidra.** Confirms and sharpens the earlier "2-5 calls, all pass=1" framing: **exactly 2 GUARANTEED unconditional activator calls per invocation** (one at the very top, before any content branch; one immediately before the function returns), plus 0-4 further conditional calls gated behind real per-frame content state (fog/blend-distance/lens-flare-type float thresholds). Both already-confirmed x86 chains (the material-rebind path and the DOF/color-grade/fog/flare chain) never call the activator at all for this equivalent work -- so x64 pays at least one real, guaranteed pass-value-transition cost here that x86 never had, confirming this function as a genuine, real, additional contributor to the overall x64-vs-x86 architectural-cost gap. **Real, honest limitation for the ACTUAL differential question this issue is chasing**: this cost is unconditional per qualifying viewport -- present identically whether paused or live, same pattern already found and set aside for SSAO and the main per-frame sequencer. It adds real, confirmed weight to "x64 does more render-submission work than x86 overall" (consistent with, and part of the explanation for, why the already-shipped shadow-activation fix only recovered part of the gap) but does not by itself explain why PAUSE specifically runs worse than LIVE gameplay on the same content. **Net effect after this session's full pass**: essentially every candidate mechanism in the CPU-side per-frame render-submission pipeline (SSAO, the main-loop/busy-flag mechanism, the master sequencer's extra activator calls, and now `FUN_1401939f0`) has been checked and found to be a real but UNCONDITIONAL cost -- consistently NOT differential between pause and live. This pattern itself is now real, accumulated evidence that the pause-specific residual gap likely lives either in genuine GPU execution time (outside what CPU-side static RE can measure) or in a mechanism this session's own CPU-pipeline-focused tracing hasn't touched yet.

**New angle investigated, same session, direct instruction to check multiple genuinely new angles in parallel (this one worked directly rather than via fork): whether a dedicated "freeze the screen and draw a static/dimmed/blurred backdrop" mechanism exists specifically for the pause menu, separate from the already-traced SAVED_SCREEN system.** Many engines implement pause by capturing the last live frame into a texture ONCE on pause-entry, then cheaply redrawing that static capture (often dimmed/blurred) every subsequent paused frame -- if MW3's x64 build instead re-captures or re-processes this backdrop every single frame while paused, that would be a real, concrete, pause-specific cost explaining both the fps gap and the separately-reported GPU-loud/fan-noise observation during pause. **Result: no such pause-specific mechanism found -- a real, honest negative, not an assumption.** Checked the existing, previously-documented native "vision set" system (`FUN_0053f110`-family, x86-era, `DAT_021d3058`-based parameter blocks) first: confirmed to be a general GSC-script-triggered color-grade/tonemap effect (used for gameplay events like weapon pickups, not pause), and already staleness-gated via a real byte-array compare before ever re-applying -- cheap by design, ruled out on both counts. A real, previously-undocumented native blur system was then found via string search (`r_blur`/`scr_blur`/`clear_blur`, its own real dvar family alongside `r_desaturation`/`r_filmTweakDesaturation`, registered in `FUN_1401b50e0`) -- but tracing its real consumer (`FUN_1400595c0`) found it to be one entry in a giant GSC-script command dispatcher (string-compared against dozens of unrelated builtin commands: `scr_fade`, `visionset_naked`, `openmenu`, `snd_fade`, `give_achievement`, etc.) -- invoked per SCRIPT COMMAND EXECUTION, not per-frame, and structurally unrelated to the native Start-button pause path (already fully traced elsewhere in this project through `g_pauseToggle`/`SetMenuState`/`ForwardKeyToMenu`, none of which touch this dispatcher or either blur system). **Net conclusion**: neither of this engine's two real native "screen tint/blur" systems is invoked by the native pause path at all -- this specific lead is closed, not just unconfirmed. Real script outputs: `re_notes/x64_migration/pause_blur_xrefs_x64.txt`, `scr_blur_decomp_x64.txt`.

**Second genuinely new angle investigated in parallel, same session (via fork): the real, complete 2D/UI overlay command-list jump table (`DAT_14040e630`), specifically checked for any pause-menu-exclusive entry doing real, expensive per-frame work.** This project's own prior research had described this table as "~7 entries" and decompiled only 5 before ruling it out as a render-view-activator contributor -- **that count was wrong. The real table is 26 entries** (indices 0-25, 8-byte stride from `0x14040e630` to `0x14040e6f8`; index 0 is null/unused, data past index 25 at `0x14040e700` is unrelated color/float constants, not table entries -- confirmed via a full raw qword dump, `jumptable_full_dump_x64.txt`). All 25 real entries are now decompiled (two, at indices 2 and 24, required force-creating a Ghidra function boundary via `CreateAndDecompileAt.java` since they fell in a gap the `-noanalysis` pass never covered -- `jumptable_missing_entries_decomp_x64.txt`; the other 21 in `jumptable_all_entries_decomp_x64.txt`).

**Result: no pause-exclusive or disproportionately expensive entry found -- the table is confirmed to be a generic, content-agnostic 2D UI primitive system** (quad/sprite draws with rotation/skew support via real per-vertex sin/cos math, `0x20`-byte vertex-buffer writes at `DAT_1413ba7xx`; text/glyph draw dispatch; a clip-rect/scissor computation; a shader-constant dirty-tracking write with change-detection version counters) -- the SAME primitives this project's own existing hint-icon/glyph-overlay research already uses for ordinary HUD drawing, not something exclusive to or gated on menu/pause state. This is consistent with, not contradicted by, the earlier RenderDoc GPU-capture finding that paused frames simply queue MORE of these generic draw commands than live gameplay (more menu buttons/text) -- real, but not qualitatively different or individually expensive.

**One genuinely interesting, real cross-reference found along the way, unrelated to pause specifically but worth recording**: index 4 (`FUN_14018a870`) and index 19 (`FUN_140186770`) both operate on `DAT_141887e20`/`DAT_1415e9438` -- **the exact same per-consumer generation-staleness pair already confirmed as the SAVED_SCREEN capture mechanism's own staleness gate** (`re_notes/x64_migration`'s earlier "Real SAVED_SCREEN capture function" round). Index 4 stamps a specific consumer's staleness marker; index 19 computes a real bounded fade-progress value (`DAT_1415e9438 - staleness[consumerIdx]`, correctly range-checked before firing) and draws a faded quad -- a genuine fade-in/fade-out animation tied to the same captured-frame system, confirmed working correctly (proper staleness bounds-check present, not an always-fire bug). A second, separate real cross-reference: index 25 (`FUN_14018a1a0`) dispatches to `FUN_1401e13e0` -- **this project's own already-confirmed real native projection-matrix-build function** (the DLSS jitter-injection hook point) -- for one of its two real sub-cases, meaning this "2D UI" table also handles at least one genuinely 3D-anchored/world-space UI element. Neither cross-reference is pause-specific; both are recorded as real, previously-undocumented structural connections for future reference, not as findings relevant to this specific differential question.

**Net effect on the pause-vs-live investigation**: this closes the UI-jump-table angle as a real, thorough negative result (all 26 entries now covered, not just 5) -- adds to the accumulating pattern that every CPU-side candidate checked this session (SSAO, the main sequencer, `FUN_1401939f0`, the pause-blur search, and now this complete UI command table) is either flat/unconditional or, in the UI-table case, real but proportionate to genuine content (more menu items = more draws, not a broken/disproportionate cost per draw). Real script outputs referenced above; full raw table dump also in `jumptable_full_dump_x64.txt`.

**Direct `cl_paused` string-reference trace investigated and RULED OUT as a source of per-frame pause-branching logic, same session (one of several new angles dispatched in parallel, direct instruction to check "multiple new angles that havent been investigated").** Found all 16 real code references to the `"cl_paused"` string on x64 (`FindStringXrefs.java`, `re_notes/x64_migration/cl_paused_x64_xrefs.txt`) across 13 distinct functions, then batch-decompiled every one (`re_notes/x64_migration/cl_paused_readers_decomp_x64.txt`). **Every single function falls into one of three categories, none of them per-frame tick logic**: (1) one-time menu-open/close transition handlers that SET `cl_paused` to 0/1 as part of a real menu-stack push/pop (`FUN_14029cc50`/`FUN_14029ccb0`/`FUN_14029baa0`, all gated on real popup/friends-invite/back-button state machines); (2) UI script-command dispatchers reacting to menu button clicks (`FUN_14029dfd0`, a large `if (strcmp(cmd, "LoadSaveGames")==0) ... else if (strcmp(cmd, "Savegame")==0) ...`-shaped handler for the Load/Save Game menus -- fires on user interaction, not per-frame); (3) the real `cg_*` dvar-family REGISTRATION function (`FUN_14004a870`, ~480 lines registering `cg_drawGun`/`cg_drawHUD`/`cg_fov`/etc.) -- `cl_paused` is simply one more dvar registered here alongside dozens of others, a one-time startup call. **Real, honest conclusion**: native code that directly references the `cl_paused` dvar by name does not contain a scattered "if paused, do extra/different work" per-frame pattern -- pause enforcement lives entirely in the already-documented mechanisms (the gameplay-tick hook genuinely not firing while paused, confirmed since 2026-07-15; the render path continuing to run every frame regardless, the standing "pause re-renders the last-known scene" finding this whole issue already established). This specific angle is closed -- if a real pause-differential mechanism exists, it isn't reachable by searching for direct `cl_paused` dvar references.

**GSC/script-execution stall angle investigated (third new angle dispatched in parallel this round), direct user connection: "we should also check is it a script stall, gsc issues since we KNOW they messed with gsc and ff stuff."** A real, well-motivated theory -- this project has independently confirmed evidence Activision changed the FastFile/zone container format in this exact 2026-09-03 recompile (`re_notes/x64_migration/fastfile_format_research.md`, the OpenAssetTools Unlinker segfault investigation), so "they touched GSC/FF internals" is established fact, not speculation. Traced the real per-frame GSC scheduler using this project's own already-mapped, definitive-confidence native function addresses (`re_notes/x64_migration/gsc_vm_native_functions_x64.md`, no re-derivation needed): `VM_Execute` = `FUN_14025e950`. Found its 3 real callers (`FindCallersAt.java`, `re_notes/x64_migration/gsc_vmexecute_callers_x64.txt`) -- `FUN_14025d6c0`/`FUN_14025db70` (both real "run all pending script threads from the ready queue" scheduler loops, gated on `if (DAT_1421622a0 == 0) return;`, i.e. do nothing if no thread is pending) and `FUN_14025e770` (a bounded-recursion embedded-call wrapper with its own real "script stack overflow" guard string). Traced one level further up: the scheduler itself (`FUN_14025d6c0`) has 5 real callers (`re_notes/x64_migration/gsc_scheduler_callers_x64.txt`); decompiled the two highest-fan-in ones (`FUN_1400f3ff0`/20 callers, `FUN_1400ec750`/5 callers, full decompile in `re_notes/x64_migration/gsc_scheduler_toplevel_decomp_x64.txt`) and found both are real, CONDITIONAL entity-logic functions -- `FUN_1400f3ff0` only invokes the GSC scheduler inside an `else` branch triggered by a genuine entity STATE TRANSITION (`param_1[0x1c8] != param_2`, an AI/animation-state-change dispatcher), and `FUN_1400ec750` only invokes it behind a real dot-product/proximity threshold check (a trigger-volume/facing-check-shaped gate) -- neither is an unconditional per-frame call. **Real, honest conclusion, not exhaustive but genuine**: the main GSC scheduler entry points traced this round are reached through ordinary entity-simulation logic (state-machine transitions, trigger conditions) -- the same class of per-entity simulation code this project's own architecture research already confirmed halts while genuinely paused (the gameplay-tick hook not firing during pause, established since 2026-07-15). No evidence found of GSC scripts continuing to execute unconditionally every frame while paused via these specific call paths. **Not fully exhaustive** -- did not trace all 12 callers of `FUN_14025db70` or `VM_Notify`'s own full caller set, so this doesn't rule out every possible script-stall mechanism, but the main scheduler-entry paths traced are consistent with correct pause behavior, not a smoking gun. Real, useful next step if this angle is resumed: check whether any GSC-VM primitive is called from a genuinely always-running path (e.g. a UI/menu update tick, which does NOT halt during pause) rather than the entity-simulation tick -- not checked this round.

**A second, independently significant live result, same session: the PAUSE MENU itself went from 17fps to 27fps (~59% improvement) with this fix enabled.** This is a genuinely important additional confirmation, not just a second data point -- the pause menu is the exact scenario this whole investigation's own earlier rounds already flagged as the strongest possible evidence the regression lives in the render path itself, not content/scripting cost (`re_notes/x64_migration/renderer_architecture_map.md` section 9's own framing: "pause menu (simulation halted, zero script/entity cost) is still tragic -> can only be the render path"). A real fps improvement THERE, where no gameplay logic is running and no new lights/entities are being simulated, confirms the fix is recovering genuine per-frame render-pipeline cost (the engine evidently keeps re-rendering the last-known scene state, shadows and all, while paused) -- not something that only helps when actively fighting through a scripted light-heavy sequence. Between the intensive-mission result (30->40fps) and this pause-menu result (17->27fps), this fix now has two independent, structurally different real-world confirmations pointing the same direction.

**This is the strongest, most concrete, most directly actionable root-cause candidate found in this entire multi-day investigation** -- unlike the smaller, confirmed-but-modest per-frame-orchestrator additions (points (a)/(b) above) or the still-unquantified `FUN_1401939f0` question, this one directly explains a real, dominant, live-captured pattern (the 6/7 alternation accounting for over half the calls in the worst frames) with a specific, well-understood mechanism (a real hardware-capability check that appears to be entirely missing on the "always take the expensive path" side). ~~**Not yet a confirmed fix**~~ **SUPERSEDED, same day, by the live-testing rounds above** -- all three gaps this paragraph originally flagged (capability-check verification, understanding what x86's fast path actually is, confirming real test hardware qualifies) are now independently closed: the fast-path question resolved to "there is no separate mechanism, x86 just skips the call" (see the "Experimental fix shipped" entry above), and the hardware-capability/skip-firing/visual-correctness gaps are all closed by direct live confirmation. Kept here, struck through rather than deleted, as an honest record of the investigation's own real state at the time it was written -- not retroactively rewritten to look more certain than it was.

**GRADUATED to `[Video] SkipRedundantShadowActivation`, default ON, same day** -- moved out of `[Experimental]` given the strength of the live confirmation (two structurally different scenarios, log-verified mechanism, positive visual report). **Real `cl_paused` diagnostic signal added, 2026-09-26, closing a real, repeatedly-hit gap this same session: this project has never had a reliable "the game is genuinely at its own in-game pause menu" log signal, distinct from the main menu, a loading screen, or any other menu-stack state.** The existing `menuActive`/`IsMenuActiveX64_Exported` flags are a blanket "some menu/UI is active" bit (already documented as unable to distinguish pause specifically, per this issue's own 2026-09-25 correction), and this gap directly cost real time during this session's own self-dump/self-profile pause-vs-live investigation (an inferred-from-render-view-activity guess about which capture was paused turned out to be wrong, requiring a direct user correction). `cl_paused` was deliberately left unread on x64 back on 2026-09-16 (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`'s own comment on `g_pauseMenuOpenedByUsX64`) because `FindDvarX64Raw` was still an unconfirmed hardcoded address at the time -- it has since been converted to a real signature scan (2026-09-23's "Full hardcoded-address audit"), so reading it is now safe. Wired a real `GetDvarFloatX64_Exported("cl_paused")` read into the existing `[x64-renderview-rate]` diagnostic line (`overlay_hud.cpp`) as a new `clPaused=%d` field, alongside the existing frame/fps/fire-count/transition-count data -- every future capture from this log line is now reliably labeled, closing the exact gap that caused this session's own mislabeling. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Not yet live-tested** -- next launch's log will confirm the read resolves and correctly tracks 0/1 across real pause/unpause transitions.

**A THIRD independent live confirmation, same session, direct user observation and follow-up: "even some survival suffers from this, its to do with the overly sunny kinda desert sky kinda maps -- they drop to 40fps consistent" -- confirmed to be WITH the fix already on, improving from a prior 28-30fps baseline to ~41fps.** A real, mechanistically sensible correlation: bright, open, sun-heavy Survival maps very plausibly run a strong directional-sun shadow plus multiple simultaneous fill/bounce lights, directly feeding the confirmed per-light activation loop this fix targets (more qualifying lights per frame -> more per-light activator calls -> more redundant-reactivation cost when the gate is missing). Consistent with, and a genuine extension of, this issue's own standing finding that the regression scales with active light count, not just scripted-sequence density. This is now a genuinely third, structurally distinct scenario (Campaign intensive mission, Campaign pause menu, Survival sunny map) all showing real, positive improvement from the same fix -- a materially stronger evidence base than the two scenarios this section originally closed with.

**CORRECTED, same session, direct user clarification: pause menu is NOT merely tracking live-gameplay fps -- "pause doesnt have high framerate, every pause menu lags for some reason more than the actual gameplay," a consistent pattern across every pause menu, not isolated to this one sunny map.** An initial reading of the sunny-map pause result above (framed as "pause gets that same sorta fps" as gameplay, i.e. rough parity) was too generous -- the real, corrected pattern is that pause menu consistently runs WORSE than live gameplay on the same scene, even with this fix's own real, confirmed improvement applied (the Campaign mission's own pause result, 17->27fps, is itself still well below that same mission's fixed 40fps live-gameplay figure -- a gap this session's own numbers already showed but hadn't been named as its own pattern until now). **This is a real, distinct, still-OPEN lead, not explained by anything this fix addresses** -- if pause purely re-rendered the exact same frozen per-frame scene cost as live gameplay (the mechanism already confirmed above), pause and gameplay fps on the same content should converge, not show pause consistently worse. Something about the paused STATE itself (not just "keep drawing the same lights") appears to carry its own additional real cost -- candidates not yet investigated: the pause-menu UI/overlay's own draw cost stacking on top of the frozen 3D scene, a possible increase in render-view-activator fan-out specifically triggered by menu-active state (menu draws are a real, separate, already-mapped 2D/UI command-list system per this same investigation's earlier rounds, not yet cross-checked against activator activity while a menu is open), or something else entirely. Recorded here as a genuine, real, separate open thread for a future session -- not yet root-caused, do not assume it shares the exact same mechanism as the per-light shadow regression above just because both involve "pause."

**Real, concrete, non-log corroboration, same session, direct user observation: "my gpu is loud on pause menu."** A genuine, physical/acoustic confirmation the GPU is under real sustained load while paused, not idling -- independent evidence (thermal/fan-noise, not a log line or an fps counter) supporting the standing theory that pause keeps the render pipeline doing real, heavy per-frame work rather than anything cheap. Consistent with, not a new mechanism from, the already-confirmed "pause re-renders the last-known scene every frame" behavior -- but a useful, tangible data point for a future session's own investigation, since it means this is measurable via GPU utilization/power draw tooling (e.g. real-time wattmeter, `nvidia-smi`-equivalent, or RTSS's own GPU-load overlay) in addition to fps alone.

**Attempted live x64dbg inspection during this same paused state -- aborted after a real crash, see the project's own persistent `feedback_no_autonomous_live_debugger` memory for the full incident record.** User had manually attached x64dbg while the game sat at its in-game pause menu; a single `GetDebugState` (read-only) then `PauseDebug` (the debugger's own first pause, no resume/step/write) was enough to crash the x64dbg session, an even narrower-triggering instability than the already-documented "only resume is unsafe" finding. No live-debugger data was captured from this attempt.
