**User's working theory, same session: "must be anti debug measure this is why we historically avoided debug since the x64 switch."** Retrospectively connects every live-debugger-instability incident since the 2026-09-03 x86->x64 recompile (the 2026-09-15 cdb black-screen, the 2026-09-16/17 x64dbg resume-crashes, this session's pause-crash) into one real anti-debug protection introduced by the recompile, rather than independent tooling bugs. Plausible and worth taking seriously, but one piece of standing counter-evidence doesn't fit cleanly: x64dbg also crashed on resume against `Unlinker.exe`, an unrelated offline CLI tool with no anti-debug of its own -- so this can't be the whole explanation, even if it's a real contributor against the live game process specifically. A fresh x64dbg snapshot build (commit `9c2c21a`, 2026-04-20) was installed this session to `D:\Tools\x64dbg` (the prior install, commit `9c8ca1c`/2026-05-27, backed up to `D:\Tools\x64dbg_old_20260527_9c8ca1c`) to test whether a different build changes this behavior. **Retested same day -- same crash** ("nah it did the same crash"), ruling out "build-specific x64dbg regression" as the explanation and strengthening the anti-debug read, since the instability now reproduces across two independent x64dbg builds/commits against this same game process. Full detail: the project's own persistent `feedback_no_autonomous_live_debugger` memory record.

**Separately, real, additional corroborating evidence for the whole investigation's core thesis, direct user observation: "all maps and missions that in x86 ran basically no diff from each other."** If the SAME content (same maps/missions, unchanged assets) ran with roughly flat, uniform performance on the original x86 binary, but the x64 binary shows wide, content-dependent swings (a sunny Survival map dropping into the 30s/40s, a specific Campaign mission needing this exact fix to recover from 30 to 40fps, pause consistently underperforming gameplay) -- that variance itself is strong, further evidence the regression is x64-introduced, not an inherent property of specific map content both architectures would be expected to suffer under equally. Consistent with, and reinforcing, this whole issue's own central finding (the 2-vs-40 real static caller count, the missing hardware-capability gate) rather than a new independent claim -- the same underlying mechanism (more real render-view activator work scaling with active light count) would naturally produce exactly this kind of "some content hit harder than others" pattern that x86's own cheaper, gated path never allowed to manifest at all.

**Real memory-dump investigation plan for the still-open pause-vs-gameplay lead, direct user instruction, 2026-09-26: capture full self-triggered memory dumps (F9, `TriggerSelfMemoryDumpX64`, already-existing infrastructure -- see `d3d9_hook.cpp`) during both live gameplay AND paused, at the same spot, across multiple scenarios (the Campaign intensive mission, the sunny Survival map, plus intensive maps/missions generally) -- "we will do the same in those intensive maps and missions."** No new code needed; this reuses the exact same safe, proven, no-external-handle self-dump technique already built for the x86-era crash investigations. Dumps land next to `proxy_d3d9.log`. Plan: diff real per-thread call-stack/state between a live-gameplay dump and a paused dump at the same in-game moment, across several scenario pairs, looking for what's genuinely different about the render thread's own work while paused.

**Real tooling bug found and fixed the same day, first real capture attempt**: the first two real F9 dumps came out at 10.1GB and 12.2GB respectively (Task Manager showed `iw5sp.exe`'s own working set at only ~2.4GB at the time) -- `MiniDumpWithFullMemory` captures every committed page in the process's address space, including this project's own `IwdReadAccelEnabled` feature's real memory-mapped `.iwd` archive file views (committed virtual memory, never shown in Task Manager's resident-working-set column, but still fully captured by a full-memory dump). **Direct user report: this was also crashing/hanging the game** -- `MiniDumpWriteDump` runs synchronously on the calling thread (inside the `WndProc` F9 handler), so writing 10+GB to disk blocked the whole game long enough to look and act like a genuine crash. Direct user instruction: "we just need the bounded game memory... weve identified it lives in subsections of the memory based on x86 approach." Fixed by switching `TriggerSelfMemoryDumpX64` from `MiniDumpWithFullMemory` to `MiniDumpWithDataSegs | MiniDumpWithPrivateReadWriteMemory | MiniDumpWithHandleData | MiniDumpWithThreadInfo | MiniDumpWithFullMemoryInfo` -- captures the process's own private (not file-backed/shared) read-write memory, module `.data`/`.bss` globals, and full per-thread context/stack-walk data, while excluding the giant mapped-file views that bloated the first two captures. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Not yet live-tested** -- next F9 press will confirm both the real size reduction and that the game no longer hangs/crashes on capture. The two original oversized dumps (`selfdump_20260925_151152.dmp`/`_151548.dmp`, ~22.3GB combined) are left on disk for now, per direct instruction ("leave for now but note for deletion later") -- flagged here as a real, pending cleanup item, not yet actioned.

Not yet executed as of this entry -- awaiting the user's own captured live-gameplay/paused dump pairs using the fixed, bounded-size capture.

**Second real tooling bug found and fixed, same day, follow-up capture attempts**: the bounded-size fix above worked cleanly for the main-menu and live-Underground-gameplay captures, but three consecutive Underground-**paused** capture attempts (`selfdump_20260925_152418.dmp`/`_152637.dmp`/`_152744.dmp`) each came out as tiny, unusable ~250KB files -- `MiniDumpWriteDump` was failing with `GetLastError=2147942487` (`0x80070057` = `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`) specifically in this one scenario, while the identical flag combination worked fine elsewhere. Two real bugs found on review: (1) `GetLastError()` was being read AFTER `CloseHandle(hFile)` in the failure branch -- a second Win32 API call between the real failure and reading its error code, which can silently clobber the true value; (2) no fallback existed at all, so any failure meant a totally empty capture for that scenario with nothing to analyze afterward. Fixed: `GetLastError()` is now captured immediately after `MiniDumpWriteDump` returns, before any other API call; if the full flag combo (`MiniDumpWithDataSegs | MiniDumpWithPrivateReadWriteMemory | MiniDumpWithHandleData | MiniDumpWithThreadInfo | MiniDumpWithFullMemoryInfo`) fails, the function now retries once with a smaller, more conservative combo (`MiniDumpWithDataSegs | MiniDumpWithPrivateReadWriteMemory` only -- the two flags that have never failed in any capture so far), and the log line now distinguishes all three outcomes (clean full-combo success, fallback-combo success with the original error recorded, or total failure with both error codes recorded) rather than one generic pass/fail message. `MiniDumpWithHandleData`/`MiniDumpWithFullMemoryInfo` are the prime suspects for the real root cause (documented dbghelp.dll edge cases around handle-table/thread-info state specifically tied to unusual process states like an open menu/paused sim) but the actual root cause of WHY the full combo fails only while paused remains unconfirmed -- the fallback exists specifically so a future capture attempt doesn't come back empty-handed either way. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed.

**Retested same day -- round 1's fallback did NOT fix the pause failure, and introduced a real NEW regression on top: the previously-reliable LIVE-gameplay capture also failed this time ("the live one failed where it didnt before, thats a regression").** Two new tiny (~244KB) dumps, both logging `MiniDumpWriteDump FAILED even with fallback flags (first=2147942487, fallback=2147942487)` -- i.e. the round-1 FALLBACK combo (`MiniDumpWithDataSegs | MiniDumpWithPrivateReadWriteMemory`, with neither `MiniDumpWithHandleData` nor `MiniDumpWithFullMemoryInfo`) failed with the IDENTICAL `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` as the full combo -- ruling those two flags out as the specific culprit, since a combo without either one still fails the same way. **Root cause of the live-capture regression, found on review: both attempts reused the SAME file handle.** A failed `MiniDumpWriteDump` call can partially write to the file before erroring, so retrying on that same handle risks feeding a corrupted/appended file into the second attempt -- plausibly explaining why even the live-gameplay case, previously reliable, broke once a same-handle retry was added. **Round 2 fix**: each of now THREE tiers (full combo, reduced combo, and a new bare `MiniDumpNormal` minimal tier -- no extra flags at all, the most universally-supported combination DbgHelp has, still enough for real thread stacks/module list/exception info) opens its own fresh, truncated (`CREATE_ALWAYS`) file handle rather than reusing one across attempts. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Retested same day -- succeeded, via the new `minimal` (`MiniDumpNormal`) tier, on BOTH captures.** Both captures (`selfdump_20260925_155744.dmp`/`_155750.dmp`) still had the `full` and `reduced` tiers fail identically (`first=2147942487`, `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`) before `minimal` finally succeeded. **Correction to an inference made while first writing this up**: the surrounding log context for `_155750.dmp` showed `[x64-renderview-select-diag]` actively cycling view indices every frame right up to the capture -- initially read as evidence this specific capture was LIVE gameplay, not paused. **Direct user correction: "nope the last last one was pause."** That inference was invalid, not just wrong -- render-view activity continuing is exactly what this whole issue's own already-confirmed finding predicts DURING pause too (pause keeps re-rendering the scene every frame, the core regression this issue tracks), so it was never a valid live-vs-paused discriminator in the first place. There is currently no reliable log signal in this codebase for "the game is at its own in-game pause menu" specifically (`menuActiveGateFlag`/`DAT_1406e2550` tracks a DIFFERENT menu-active concept, evidently not this one, since it read `0x00000000` during a confirmed-paused capture) -- a real, standing documentation/tooling gap worth closing before this investigation leans on log-inferred state again. **Net effect: the "pause vs. live" question for whether the tier-1/tier-2 failure is pause-specific is back to genuinely unresolved** -- `_155750.dmp` is now confirmed paused (user's direct report), `_155744.dmp`'s actual state is unconfirmed either way, and the earlier-in-session success (`selfdump_20260925_152317.dmp`, 2.7GB, ~15:23) also has unconfirmed pause/live state. The session-memory-growth lead (`workingSetMB=5535.4` at the time of the successful capture, vs. whatever the footprint was at 15:23) remains a real, independent, still-plausible correlate regardless of this correction -- not retracted, just no longer treated as having ruled out a pause-specific mechanism too. Both successful minimal-tier dumps were opened via `mcp-windbg` (static, offline, no live attach) and confirmed usable: real thread lists recovered, 59 live threads including a full DXVK/Vulkan worker pool (`dxvk-submit`/`dxvk-queue`/`dxvk-cs`/`dxvk-descriptor`, several `dxvk-shader-l`/`n`/`h` compiler threads, `dxvk-frame`) and an active Streamline `sl.log` thread -- real, independent confirmation of heavy background GPU-driver/Vulkan activity, consistent with the separately-reported GPU-loud-during-pause observation now that `_155750.dmp` is confirmed itself to be a paused capture. **Next step for a future round**: a reliable, explicit "game is at its own in-game pause menu" log signal is needed before pause-vs-live can be inferred from the log at all -- consider adding one directly (e.g. logging the real pause-menu state bit this project's own pause/unpause work already tracks) rather than inferring it from unrelated diagnostics. Once that exists, re-run the fresh-relaunch-vs-grown-session memory test with reliable state labels on each capture.

**Both minimal-tier dumps compared thread-by-thread, same session -- byte-identical, no smoking gun found.** Both `_155744.dmp` and `_155750.dmp` were opened via `mcp-windbg` and every one of their 59-60 threads compared: same thread IDs, same RIP-equivalent return addresses, same wait states (`SleepConditionVariableSRW`, `WaitForSingleObject`, etc.), down to the exact instruction offset, in both dumps. Real, honest limitation identified rather than a finding: a `MiniDumpNormal` capture is a single instant, and virtually every background/worker thread is caught mid-wait at any single instant regardless of overall frame cost (a thread pool worker always sits at the identical idle wait point between jobs) -- this technique cannot show a SUSTAINED performance difference between two states, only a snapshot. Confirmed real, useful groundwork either way: 59 live threads recovered cleanly including a full DXVK/Vulkan worker pool and an active Streamline thread, real thread/module data, just not the right instrument for this specific question.

**New tool built in response, direct user proposal: "why not do a live scanning approach in our dll with stealth measures to counter anti debug etc."** A real, in-process, REPEATED sampling profiler (`self_sampling_profiler_x64.cpp`, F10) rather than a single-instant snapshot -- addresses both real limitations above in one step. **Important correction to the "stealth" framing, worth being precise about**: this tool does not attach as an external debugger at all, so it was never in the anti-debug fight the "stealth" framing implies fighting through. It uses `SuspendThread`/`GetThreadContext`/`ResumeThread` against this SAME process's own sibling threads -- a completely ordinary pattern every real sampling profiler (Superluminal, Very Sleepy, VTune) and every language runtime's GC already uses, which never calls `DebugActiveProcess`, never establishes a debug object/port, and never touches `PEB->BeingDebugged` -- the specific machinery techniques like `ThreadHideFromDebugger` actually target. So this isn't "the same technique, but stealthier" -- it's a genuinely different mechanism that was never subject to that fight in the first place, which is exactly why it should be safe where an attached x64dbg reproducibly wasn't. **What it does**: on F10, samples every other thread's RIP every 20ms for 3 seconds (refreshing the thread list each round, since this project's own background threads and the game's worker pool come and go), resolves each hit against a module list snapshotted once at start (no DbgHelp symbol resolution at all, sidestepping whatever's failing inside `MiniDumpWriteDump`'s own internal walk entirely), and writes a plain-text report: per thread, its top 5 most-common module+RVA hits by percentage across all samples -- a real, coarse "where is time actually going" answer built from nothing but ordinary same-process thread introspection. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Live report same day: "doesnt work ive been pressing f10" -- real bug found and fixed.** No `selfprofile_*.txt` files and no `[self-profile]` log lines existed at all, confirming the trigger never fired rather than firing and failing silently. Root cause: a bare F10 press (no Alt/Ctrl held) is delivered by Windows as `WM_SYSKEYDOWN`, not `WM_KEYDOWN` -- a well-known legacy quirk, since F10 alone also activates the menu-bar/system-menu context in a normal Win32 app. This project's own keybind-capture editor (same file, line ~525) already handles both message types for the identical reason -- the new F10 trigger just didn't follow that existing precedent. Fixed by checking `(msg == WM_KEYDOWN || msg == WM_SYSKEYDOWN)`. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Live report same day: "doesnt work ive been pressing f10" -- real bug found and fixed.** No `selfprofile_*.txt` files and no `[self-profile]` log lines existed at all, confirming the trigger never fired rather than firing and failing silently. Root cause: a bare F10 press (no Alt/Ctrl held) is delivered by Windows as `WM_SYSKEYDOWN`, not `WM_KEYDOWN` -- a well-known legacy quirk, since F10 alone also activates the menu-bar/system-menu context in a normal Win32 app. This project's own keybind-capture editor (same file, line ~525) already handles both message types for the identical reason -- the new F10 trigger just didn't follow that existing precedent. Fixed by checking `(msg == WM_KEYDOWN || msg == WM_SYSKEYDOWN)`. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed.

**Retested same day -- F10 fires correctly now, two real captures (69 and 73 rounds, 61 threads each) -- but no usable signal: essentially every thread sat 89-100% idle in `ntdll.dll` wait syscalls in both captures, with only scattered single-sample hits inside `iw5sp.exe`/`d3d9.dll`/`nvoglv64.dll`.** Real, honest limitation, not a tool failure: at the original 20ms sampling interval, a sampler mostly just catches the GAPS between frames (a few ms of real work at this project's own typical 100+fps under Vulkan) rather than the real work itself -- idle-between-frames is genuinely the majority state most of the time even under real, sustained load. Two improvements made in response, direct instruction ("do a multi second scan"): (1) sampling interval tightened from 20ms to 5ms, so real per-frame work has far more chances to actually get caught mid-execution; (2) the profile window widened from the original 3s to a genuine multi-second window (8s) so more total samples accumulate per thread, giving a real signal a better chance to rise above single-round noise (report size stays bounded regardless, since only the top 5 entries per thread are ever written); (3) real thread names added via `GetThreadDescription` (an ordinary same-process WinAPI, no debugger needed) -- DXVK names its own worker pool (`dxvk-cs`/`dxvk-submit`/`dxvk-queue`/`dxvk-frame`/`dxvk-shader-*`), so the report can now show e.g. `Thread 1234 [dxvk-cs]` instead of a bare, unidentifiable thread ID. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Retested same day with the tightened/named build -- a real, decoded signal found, then correctly ruled out as the root cause via a separate user report.** Two captures (live 160fps, paused 40fps) compared: DXVK's own `dxvk-submit` thread showed a real, measurable behavioral shift -- live spent 47.6% of samples in `NtWaitForAlertByThreadId+0x14` (DXVK's normal "waiting for real work" condition-variable idle wait) vs. 40.7% in `NtDelayExecution+0x14` (a genuine, timed Sleep call, both addresses decoded via a `dumpbin /exports` lookup against the real `ntdll.dll` on disk, not guessed), while paused flipped to 97.1% in the Sleep call and only 2.3% waiting for real work. Initially investigated as a strong lead (a striking coincidental match to an already-existing code comment in `frame_pacing_x64.cpp` predicting exactly this signature) -- but the project's own existing `[frame-pacing-diag]` log line showed `com_maxfps` stayed at `0` (unlimited) for the entire session, meaning this project's own `LimitVisibleFrame` pacer never actually ran, ruling out this project's own code as the source. A follow-up dive into the `MW32011DXVK` fork's own source (`dxvk_queue.cpp`'s submit thread, `d3d9_swapchain.cpp`'s `maxFrameRate` limiter) to find DXVK's own internal cause was in progress when the user provided the decisive piece of context: **"this existed even on d3d9"** -- the pause-vs-live fps gap reproduces under `LegacyD3D9` too, a backend where the `dxvk-submit` thread doesn't even exist. **This correctly rules out the DXVK submit-thread Sleep behavior as the root cause of the overall regression** -- it's a real, Vulkan-specific artifact worth keeping on record, but not the shared mechanism behind the actual bug, which must be something common to both backends (native engine behavior, or one of this project's own backend-agnostic hooks) rather than anything DXVK-internal. Investigation redirected accordingly -- the CPU sampling profiler itself remains a real, working tool for whatever the next lead turns out to be, this specific thread just isn't it.

**New tool built in response, direct user instruction: "how bout we do something weve never done on this proj, dump gpu to disk."** The CPU sampling profiler's own real limit (no thread shows sustained work in either live or paused captures -- consistent with real background threads correctly idling either way, but structurally unable to distinguish "genuinely idle" from "correctly blocked waiting on the GPU") called for a fundamentally different instrument: real GPU-side capture, not more CPU thread sampling. New `renderdoc_capture_x64.cpp` (F11) integrates RenderDoc's official, real, widely-used in-application API -- `renderdoc_app.h` fetched VERBATIM from the official `github.com/baldurk/renderdoc` repo (MIT license, vendored under `proxy_d3d9/third_party/renderdoc/`) rather than hand-written from memory, since its function-pointer struct layout is safety-critical to get byte-exact (a wrong field order would call an arbitrary wrong function through the resolved API table). **Real, load-bearing timing finding**: RenderDoc's own documentation requires `RENDERDOC_GetAPI()` to run BEFORE any graphics device/context is created, or its Vulkan layer can't hook `vkCreateInstance` and capture silently won't work -- the correct call site turned out to be the TOP of this DLL's own exported `Direct3DCreate9` forwarder (`dllmain.cpp`), immediately before calling through to the real/DXVK `Direct3DCreate9` (which is where DXVK creates its actual `VkInstance` lazily). Deliberately NOT called from `DllMain`'s own `DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH`, even though that would be earlier still -- this project has a real, live-reproduced precedent (`TryInitStreamlineX64`, moved out of `DllMain` after a confirmed loader-lock hang) for exactly this class of mistake. `Direct3DCreate9` runs on the game's own calling thread well after `DllMain` has returned, satisfying RenderDoc's own requirement while keeping the same safety profile as every other post-`DllMain` hook in this project. F11 calls `TriggerCapture()` (captures the next frame automatically, no manual Start/End bracketing needed), writing a real `.rdc` file beside the game exe -- openable in RenderDoc's own UI for a genuine, authoritative, per-draw-call/per-event GPU timeline, directly comparable between a live-gameplay frame and a paused-menu frame. Degrades cleanly and logs clearly if RenderDoc isn't installed (checks a bare `renderdoc.dll` on PATH, then the default `C:\Program Files\RenderDoc\` install location) -- **RenderDoc itself is NOT vendored/bundled, the user must install it separately (free, official, renderdoc.org) for this to do anything**. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. **Not yet live-tested** -- next step is installing RenderDoc, confirming the `[gpu-capture]` startup log line shows successful init, then capturing one frame live and one paused via F11 for direct comparison.

**A real, testable, user-proposed hypothesis investigated the same session via static RE, independent of the memory-dump plan: "what if these mf broke the resolution or something that either the lighting is drawing at or the skybox lighting or sm[shadow maps]."** Decompiled the real x64 render-target creation chain (`FUN_1401d4040`/`FUN_1401d44f0`, the same functions already tied to the render-scale tier-clamp computation per the 2026-09-24 finding) in full. **Confirmed, real, previously-undocumented finding**: every post-process/SSAO buffer this chain creates -- `$float_z`, `$post_effect_0`/`1`, `$pingpong_0`/`1`, `$ssao`/`$ssao_blurred`/`$ssao_float_z`, `$resolved_scene` -- is sized directly from `DAT_141888670`/`DAT_141888674`, the SAME render-scale-affected internal-resolution pair `InternalRenderScalePercent` overrides (confirmed via `Hook_FUN_00463820`'s own already-documented consumer chain). Only `$saved_screen` uses the separate, fixed, tier-clamped native-reference pair (`DAT_141888678`/`67c`). This is real, direct, decisive confirmation that MOST of this project's own visual-enhancement-suite render targets genuinely do scale with render-scale -- exactly the class of finding the user's hypothesis was reaching for, now confirmed rather than speculative, for this specific set of buffers.

**RESOLVED, same session, continued digging -- shadow-map creation found, and the render-scale-coupling half of the hypothesis is REFUTED, not confirmed.** The gap above (shadow-map creation code not found via direct reference search) was closed by pivoting technique -- rather than searching for references to the name-string labels, enumerated every real caller of the generic creation wrapper (`FUN_1401b92d0`) directly. This surfaced a genuinely new, previously-unexamined function this session hadn't looked at, **`FUN_1401d4440`** -- a real per-target creation helper taking width/height/format/slot-index as parameters and indexing into the SAME contiguous render-target name-pointer table (`1404d0740`-`1404d07b0`) via `(param_6 - <base>) >> 5` (a genuine 32-byte-stride struct-array index computation). Cross-checked this against `renderer_architecture_map.md`'s own prior research (Fork 3, "the render-target table's real consumer -- FOUND") before treating it as new -- that entry explicitly flagged "finding this function's own caller (the real per-target dispatch loop)" as **not yet done**, confirming `FUN_1401d4440` genuinely closes that exact, previously-open gap rather than duplicating it.

Traced `FUN_1401d4440`'s own real caller: **`FUN_1401d4e50`** -- already visible (but not previously decompiled) inside `FUN_1401d44f0`'s own body, called exactly twice (`FUN_1401d4e50(0, DAT_141888682, 2, &DAT_141bb6f40)` / `FUN_1401d4e50(1, DAT_141888680, 4, &DAT_141bb6f60)`), matching `shadowmap_large`/`shadowmap_small`'s own table position exactly. `FUN_1401d4e50` computes `height = width * <2 or 4>` internally (`param_3 = param_2 * param_3`) before forwarding to `FUN_1401d4440` -- a real, deliberate 1:2 and 1:4 aspect-ratio shadow-atlas shape, not a square shadow map.

**The decisive part**: `DAT_141888680`/`DAT_141888682` (the real shadow-map width source) are NOT the same globals `InternalRenderScalePercent` overrides (`DAT_141888670`/`674`) -- traced both to their single real writer, `FUN_1401bd1d0` (the same master resolution/tier-setup function that ALSO writes the render-scale pair, confirmed via its own full decompile), and found they come from a **different field in the same input struct**: `DAT_141888680 = *(param_1 + 0x1c)` / `DAT_141888682 = *(param_1 + 0x1e)`, versus the render-scale pair's `DAT_141888670 = *(param_1 + 4)` / `674 = *(param_1 + 0x24)` -- different offsets into the same one-time resolution-config record, not derived from each other. **This means shadow-map dimensions do NOT scale with `InternalRenderScalePercent`** -- the render-scale-coupling half of the user's own hypothesis ("what if... the skybox lighting or sm[shadow maps]" broke via a resolution mix-up) is genuinely refuted by this specific trace, not confirmed. Real, honest, not-yet-closed follow-up: where struct field `+0x1c`/`+0x1e` itself gets its value (i.e., is the shadow-map base size fixed/hardcoded, format-tier-driven, or something else) was not traced this round -- `FUN_1401bd1d0`'s own caller would be the next step if this specific sub-thread is resumed, but this isn't expected to matter for the render-scale-coupling question already answered above.

**Net effect on the broader investigation**: this doesn't add a new render-scale-coupling regression candidate, but it DOES confirm (for the second time this session, independently) that most of the OTHER post-process/SSAO buffers genuinely do scale with render-scale while shadow maps deliberately do not -- consistent with a real, intentional design distinction in the engine (shadow maps sized by content/format needs, everything else by display/render resolution) rather than an x64-introduced bug. The shadow-map-specific angle of the user's hypothesis is closed; the still-open threads remain the pause-vs-gameplay lead (awaiting the memory-dump captures) and `FUN_1401939f0`'s own real transition cost.

**Full whole-binary CPU-side static-RE sweep, 2026-09-26, direct instruction ("maybe we need to look as a whole what does the entire binary do differently") -- every remaining plausible CPU-side mechanism checked and closed, none explain the pause-vs-live differential.** Following the shadow-activation fix already shipped (`SkipRedundantShadowActivation`, confirmed live to recover part of the gap but not all of it -- pause still runs measurably worse than live gameplay on identical content), this round systematically ruled out every other CPU-side candidate:
- **SSAO** (`FUN_1401974f0`/`FUN_1401d9130` x64 vs `FUN_00417430`/`FUN_00552ac0` x86): dvar registration byte-identical; per-viewport setup logic structurally IDENTICAL on both architectures, including an ungated `r_ssaoDownsample` copy present on BOTH -- **closed, not a regression**.
- **Race-condition/busy-flag hypothesis** (direct user suspicion: "theyve accidentally created a race condition that fires 4x... im also strongly suspecting the lighting engine"): `DAT_025d6e14`(x86)/`DAT_1415e6480`(x64) is an exception-recovery flag, not a reentrancy mutex; the real main-loop functions (`FUN_0040de80` x86 / `FUN_14018a5a0` x64) are structurally IDENTICAL, both calling the render entry up to 3x per iteration through the same 3 gated conditional blocks on both architectures -- **closed as a race condition/mutex bug, but see the "DECISIVE MECHANISM FOUND" round further below: this SAME 3-gated-call-site structure is exactly what causes pause's real double render pass, once what each gate's runtime condition actually IS got traced (not just whether the same 3 call sites structurally exist on both architectures)**.
- **I/O/memory-mapping divergence**: `CreateFileMappingA`/`MapViewOfFile` present on x86 but absent from x64 traced to Steam DRM/IPC handshake only, not asset streaming -- irrelevant. `ReadFileEx` (async overlapped streaming): x64 has MORE callers (3) than x86 (1), a real, intact double-buffered reader, not a regression. `HeapAlloc`: x86's 32 callers vs x64's 2 are genuine VS2019 CRT `_malloc_base`/`_calloc_base` centralization, benign toolchain artifact -- **closed, not a regression**.
- **Whole-binary import-table diff** (`dumpbin /imports`, both binaries, custom Python diff script): found new `WINHTTP.dll`/`bcrypt.dll`/real COM init on x64, and a migration to `InitializeConditionVariable`/`SleepConditionVariableCS`/`WakeConditionVariable` absent from x86. Both traced to ground truth via parallel forks: **WinHTTP/COM** is DemonWare's own `bdHTTPWorkerWinHTTPImpl` swapping x86's bundled libcurl for WinHTTP as its real backend HTTP transport -- async/callback-driven, never blocking, deliberate modernization, unrelated to rendering. **Condition-variable migration** resolves entirely to genuine Microsoft CRT/UCRT runtime internals (`__crtLCMapStringA/W`, `__acrt_uninitialize_locks`) and SteamStub DRM-wrapper RNG init (`BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider`) -- a newer MSVC/UCRT toolchain artifact, not hand-written engine code. **Both closed, not regressions.**
- **Screen-freeze/blur-shader mechanism** (direct user angle: "maybe a blur shader or similar"): checked both VisionSet (GSC-script-triggered, staleness-gated, not per-frame) and a real, previously-undocumented native `r_blur`/`scr_blur` system (its consumer is a GSC command dispatcher invoked per script command, not per-frame) -- neither touched by pause -- **closed, not a regression**.
- **UI jump table**: full, corrected 26-entry table (not the ~7 originally estimated) fully decompiled -- a generic, content-agnostic 2D UI primitive system (quad/sprite draws, text dispatch, clip-rect math); two real cross-references found (SAVED_SCREEN staleness, the projection-matrix/DLSS-jitter function) but neither pause-specific -- **closed, exhaustive, high confidence**.
- **GSC/script-VM stalls** (mid-session addition: "ahh yes we should also check is it a script stall, gsc issues since we KNOW they messed with gsc and ff stuff"): `VM_Execute`'s real callers (the GSC scheduler) traced two levels up -- both entry points found are gated behind real conditional entity-logic (a state-transition dispatcher, a proximity/facing-check trigger), not unconditional per-frame calls -- **partial negative, honest limitation**: only 2 of 5 scheduler callers and `VM_Notify`'s own full caller set were traced; not fully exhaustive.
- **`cl_paused` direct dvar references**: all 16 real references across 13 functions are one-time menu-transition handlers, UI command dispatchers, or the `cg_*` dvar registration block -- none are per-frame tick logic -- **closed, not a regression**.

**Consistent pattern, now itself real accumulated evidence**: after this exhaustive sweep, literally everything checked is either flat/unconditional cost (paid identically whether paused or not) or genuinely unrelated to rendering at all. This pattern is the actual reason to suspect the remaining differential is real GPU EXECUTION TIME, not a CPU-side mechanism any static RE or CPU-side timing tool could ever see.

**New tool built in direct response, 2026-09-26, direct user instruction: "we need a custom gpu dump tool that tells us all info we need statically."** Neither of this session's own two "measure it directly" tools can actually see real GPU execution time: the CPU sampling profiler (F10) structurally cannot distinguish "genuinely idle" from "correctly blocked waiting on the GPU" (already documented above -- both live and paused captures showed every thread mostly idle in `ntdll.dll` wait syscalls); and RenderDoc's own `.rdc` capture, once exported to `chrome.json`, only ever contains CPU-side API-call recording timestamps, never real hardware GPU duration.

New `gpu_timing_probe_x64.cpp` (`GpuSyncMarkX64`) closes this gap directly, in-process, with no external tool or capture file: it forces a real Vulkan queue synchronization (`vkQueueWaitIdle`) at two points bracketing the real per-frame `EndScene` call (`overlay_hud.cpp`'s `Hook_EndScene`, "frame-start"/"frame-end" marks) -- because `vkQueueWaitIdle` blocks the calling CPU thread until every previously-submitted unit of GPU work on that queue has genuinely finished EXECUTING on the hardware, the real wall-clock interval between two consecutive marks is authentically GPU-inclusive, not just CPU-side recording/submission time.

**Real, deliberate tradeoff, stated plainly in the tool's own header comment and the config key's own comment**: forcing a hardware sync point removes all CPU/GPU pipelining between marks -- real, substantial fps cost while active, the same category of overhead RenderDoc's own instrumentation already demonstrated this session. Diagnostic only, never meant for normal play -- `[Experimental] GpuSyncTimingLogging`, DEFAULT OFF, Vulkan/DXVK-only (a real, harmless no-op under `LegacyD3D9`, which has no Vulkan queue to sync against at all).

**Design/implementation notes**: the real DXVK Vulkan device/queue resolution (`ResolveAndCacheDxvkVulkanHandlesX64`, via DXVK's own public `ID3D9VkInteropDevice` interop interface, `GetVulkanHandles`/`GetSubmissionQueue`) was extracted out of `streamline_integration_x64.cpp`'s existing Streamline-init path into its own standalone, idempotent function -- deliberately so this tool works without needing `StreamlineEnabled=1`. Fixed a real `LNK2019 unresolved external symbol` during this refactor: the extracted function needed external linkage (called from `d3d9_hook.cpp`), but the file's existing anonymous `namespace { ... }` block originally enclosed it, giving it internal linkage no external `extern` declaration could ever bind to -- the exact same anonymous-namespace-linkage trap this project's own commit history has hit and documented more than once before. Fixed by closing the namespace early, right before the new function. `GpuSyncMarkX64` currently brackets whole-frame timing only (v1, intentionally coarse) -- logs `elapsedMs` plus `cl_paused` (via the already-fixed `GetDvarFloatX64_Exported` accessor, closing the same "no reliable pause-state signal" gap the `[x64-renderview-rate]` line's own 2026-09-26 fix already closed) to `proxy_d3d9.log` as `[gpu-sync-mark]` lines, rate-limited (first 20 marks, then every 100th) matching this project's own standing unthrottled-log-line lesson (issue #87). Real, cheap, concrete future extension if whole-frame timing doesn't isolate the differential: additional marks at internal native-function boundaries this project's signature-scanning infrastructure already reaches (e.g. the already-hooked shadow-activation call site).

Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output: `8664 machine (x64)`), deployed to the live install. `[Experimental] GpuSyncTimingLogging=1` set live in `mw3ncp_config.ini` per this project's own standing "set config toggles live, don't wait to be asked" convention.

**Real bug found on first log check, 2026-09-26 -- the tool silently never fired the whole session despite the config being on.** `proxy_d3d9.log` showed exactly one `[gpu-sync-mark]` line all session: `vkGetDeviceProcAddr resolve FAILED`, immediately after `[dxvk-vk-handles] Resolved real DXVK Vulkan handles` succeeded a few lines earlier -- confirming the device/queue resolution itself was fine, the bug was local to this tool's own dispatch-function lookup. Root cause: the original code called `vkGetInstanceProcAddr(NULL, "vkGetDeviceProcAddr")`, assuming a NULL instance is a valid way to query a device-independent dispatch entry point. Per the real Vulkan spec, a NULL instance is ONLY valid for a small fixed set of global functions (`vkEnumerateInstanceExtensionProperties`/`LayerProperties`/`Version`, `vkCreateInstance`) -- `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` is not one of them, and DXVK's own ICD correctly returns `nullptr` for the misuse rather than tolerating it (some ICDs are more permissive here, which is likely why this pattern is sometimes seen working elsewhere). Fixed by passing the real, already-resolved `VkInstance` (`GetDxvkVkInstanceX64()`, an accessor that already existed in `streamline_integration_x64.cpp` for other consumers, cached the same way `GetDxvkVkDeviceX64()`/`GetDxvkVkQueueX64()` already are) instead of `NULL`. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), redeployed. **Retested same day, post-fix -- real data captured for the first time, confirming the tool works, but the actual live-vs-paused comparison still hasn't happened.** 51 real marks logged across one live-gameplay session, all `clPaused=0` throughout (no pause was exercised during this capture). The data itself is internally consistent and makes real architectural sense: the `frame-start->frame-end` interval (bracketing the `EndScene` call itself) is essentially free (~0.005-0.02ms) -- expected, since the hard sync already happened moments before at `frame-start`. The real cost lands in `frame-end->frame-start` (the gap between one frame's `EndScene` finishing and the next one starting, covering `Present` plus the full next frame's scene submission), which settled around a steady 34-36ms (~29fps, genuinely GPU-inclusive, consistent with on-screen fps) with two real, isolated spikes -- 370ms and 274ms, genuine multi-frame hitches, not noise. **Still not the actual payoff step**: no `clPaused=1` data exists yet to compare against -- the next capture needs to include a stretch with the in-game pause menu open, alongside a comparable live-gameplay stretch, before this tool's real live-vs-paused GPU-inclusive comparison can happen.

**REAL BUG FOUND, direct live report, 2026-09-26 -- `cl_paused` does not track x64's real in-game pause state at all: user genuinely paused during this exact capture and it stayed `clPaused=0` the entire session (confirmed via direct log grep: zero `clPaused=1` occurrences anywhere in the log, across both the `[gpu-sync-mark]` and `[x64-renderview-rate]` lines, which independently share the same `GetDvarFloatX64_Exported("cl_paused")` accessor).** `FindDvarX64Raw` itself is confirmed resolving correctly this session (`[sigscan] OK: ... resolved to 0x1402C3890`, the exact address `FindDvarX64Raw` caches, and the mechanism is reused successfully by several other already-working x64 features) -- ruling out a signature-scan failure as the cause. The read mechanism works; `cl_paused` itself is simply the wrong signal on x64, most likely because the real x64 pause-toggle chain (`FUN_1400823B0`, `g_pauseToggle`, confirmed resolved and active per `[x64-pause] Pause toggle resolved @ 0x1400823B0`) drives simulation freeze directly rather than by writing to a `cl_paused` client dvar the way x86's own console-derived pause semantics historically did -- not yet decompile-confirmed, a real, concrete next RE step if this signal is needed again, but not pursued further this round per direct instruction to use the already-available real data instead. **This retroactively corrects the 2026-09-26 `[x64-renderview-rate]` `clPaused` fix entry above** -- that fix closed a real gap in the ACCESSOR (the dvar read is now safe to call, whereas it wasn't before the 2026-09-23 signature-scan conversion), but did not, and could not have, verified `cl_paused` itself is the correct dvar to read for this purpose -- that verification is what this round's live retest was actually for, and it came back negative. Every existing log line using `clPaused=%d` (`[gpu-sync-mark]`, `[x64-renderview-rate]`) should be treated as unreliable for pause-state labeling until a real working signal is found and substituted in.

**Correction: the real per-frame data to answer this WAS already in the log -- direct re-check of `[x64-renderview-rate]` (not `[gpu-sync-mark]`, which is too rate-limited/sparse in this window to isolate the boundary) finds a dense per-frame burst that makes the pause/live boundary unambiguous without needing `clPaused` at all.** This diagnostic line switches from its normal every-30-frames sampling to logging every single frame whenever fps drops below its own internal threshold -- which happened to span exactly this test, giving a real frame-by-frame trace across the whole pause/unpause cycle:
- **Frames 1283-1423** (141 consecutive frames, the repro-scene gameplay stretch, no scene/level change): frametimes cluster tightly at 53-62ms -- **avg ~58ms (~17.2fps)**, matching the user's own "17fps" report almost exactly.
- **Frame 1424-1425**: a sharp transition spike (80.56ms -> 101.73ms) -- the real pause-menu-open hitch.
- **Frames 1425-1483** (59 consecutive frames, sustained plateau, same scene, menu now open): frametimes cluster tightly at 95-106ms -- **avg ~99ms (~10.1fps)**, matching the user's own "10fps" report almost exactly.
- **Frame 1484**: a 299.58ms spike (the unpause hitch), frames 1486-1493 settle back down, and by frame 1500 it's back to the normal ~16ms/~60fps baseline.

**Decisive result: pause ran ~99ms/frame vs. gameplay's ~58ms/frame on the IDENTICAL repro scene -- pause is ~1.71x slower, confirmed directly from real per-frame log data, not an estimate or a user-eyeballed fps counter reading.** No scene/content change occurs anywhere between the two blocks (same repro mission throughout, no level transition, no loading screen) -- this cleanly isolates the cost to pause itself, ruling out a confound where the "pause" and "gameplay" segments the user compared might have secretly also differed in scene complexity. A real, concrete future improvement, not yet made: rate-limit by TRANSITION TYPE (keep N of each direction) rather than by raw mark count, so a future capture doesn't have to get lucky the way `[x64-renderview-rate]`'s own unrelated fps-drop-triggered dense-logging behavior happened to save this one.

**DECISIVE MECHANISM FOUND, same session, direct instruction ("keep digging") -- pause runs the ENTIRE per-light shadow-dispatch loop TWICE per frame; gameplay runs it once.** `[x64-renderview-seq]` (the existing full per-frame view-index sequence dump, already logging every frame in this same fps-drop-triggered burst) gives an exact, byte-comparable trace for both states on the identical scene:
- **Frame 1300 (gameplay, 54.50ms)**: `10 10 11 11 5 5 2 2 2 2 2 14 12 6 13 2 2 2 2 2 1 [6 7]x26 8 1 1 1 1 1`
- **Frame 1450 (paused, 98.09ms)**: `10 10 11 11 5 5 2 2 2 2 2 14 12 6 13 2 2 2 2 2 1 [6 7]x26 8 1 [6 7]x26 8 1 1 1 1 1`

Byte-identical through the first `6 8 1` (the confirmed per-light shadow-dispatch loop, `FUN_140196ad0`'s own `6/7` alternation -- the exact mechanism `SkipRedundantShadowActivation` already targets). The paused frame then runs the ENTIRE `[6 7]x26 8 1` loop a SECOND time before reaching the same tail (`1 1 1 1 1`) gameplay reaches directly. This is the real cause of both the `renderViewFires`/`realTransitions` jump (56->91 / 42->76, both roughly 1.6-1.8x, tracking the ~1.71x frametime ratio) and the dedup-ratio degradation noted above (gameplay saves 25% of raw fires to dedup, pause only saves 16.5% -- consistent with a second, independent pass re-touching the same views rather than one pass simply running slower).

**Real, plausible unifying explanation, directly connecting this to the separately-found `cl_paused` gap (per direct user observation: "also cl paused not working points at a pause hook reimplemetation or move")**: a pause implementation that keeps rendering the full 3D scene twice per real frame -- rather than freezing simulation once and reusing a single captured frame -- would explain BOTH symptoms with one root cause: no client-side "simulation halted" dvar write happens because the engine isn't actually treating this as a classic sim-freeze at all, it's doing something closer to "keep rendering normally, plus one extra full pass" (consistent with this project's own already-documented `$saved_screen`/Phase-A capture-pipeline precedent for a pause-menu blurred backdrop, which would need exactly one extra full scene render to produce a background plate to blur/composite behind the menu). **Real mechanism found via direct decompile, same session, direct instruction ("keep digging"): the double render pass is driven by a real, pre-existing, generic "extra frame requested" reference count (`DAT_1418854d0`) inside the confirmed main loop (`FUN_14018a5a0`), not by anything issue #4's own already-identified shadow-activation fix introduced.** Traced the full call chain from the per-light shadow loop upward: `FUN_140196910` (the per-light loop) is called from `FUN_14018e0d0` (the confirmed once-per-viewport render-pass function, already independently documented elsewhere in this file as calling the render-view activator 4 times per invocation) only when a per-call-site gate (`param_1+0x1b0 == 1`) is set. `FUN_14018e0d0` itself has exactly 2 real callers: `FUN_140186cc0` and `FUN_14018a240` -- and `FUN_14018a240` is called from **3 separate, differently-gated call sites inside `FUN_14018a5a0`, the same confirmed main loop this file's own earlier "race-condition/busy-flag hypothesis" round examined and closed** (that earlier round only checked STRUCTURAL parity between x86/x64 -- same 3 call sites exist on both -- it never examined what each gate's real runtime condition is, which is what this round found):

- **Call site #1**, gated on `FUN_140249f50()` -- a real, separate condition (not yet decompiled this round, plausibly a "new frame/input ready" check).
- **Call site #2**, gated on `DAT_1418854d0 != 0` -- this is the real extra pass. Decompiled its setter, `FUN_1401d2c50`: a reference-counted "request an extra frame" flag (`if (DAT_1418854d0 != 0) { DAT_1418854d0++; return; } DAT_1418854d0 = 1; ...`), called from **32 separate, mostly-unrelated real call sites** scattered across the binary -- a genuine, generic, pre-existing engine mechanism (very plausibly "some UI/state-transition subsystem needs one more guaranteed frame rendered"), not something hand-built for pause specifically. A companion function, `FUN_140186bd0`, busy-waits (`Sleep(1)` loop) until this same flag clears -- confirming its real semantics are "block/extra-render until pending work finishes," consistent with a real cross-subsystem frame-request counter.

**Honest, not-yet-fully-closed gap**: which of the 32 real `FUN_1401d2c50` call sites specifically fires while the pause menu is open was NOT individually traced this round (would need checking each in turn, or a live diagnostic hook on the setter itself) -- `g_pauseToggle` (`FUN_1400823B0`) does NOT call `FUN_1401d2c50` or reference `DAT_1418854d0` directly (checked, zero references), so the real trigger is indirect, most plausibly a generic "modal UI is open" or "compositing a frozen backdrop" caller reacting to the pause menu's own broader open-state rather than a pause-specific hook. **Real reframing this finding earns, worth stating plainly**: since this project's own earlier structural check already found x86 has the identical 3-gated-call-site shape in its own main loop, x86 almost certainly ALSO double-renders while paused via the same mechanism -- meaning the double render pass itself is very likely NOT an x64-introduced regression, it's probably original, cross-architecture, by-design behavior (plausibly for a genuine blurred pause-menu backdrop capture). **What IS the real x64 regression is that each of those two renders costs more on x64 than the equivalent x86 render did** -- per the already-fixed per-light shadow-activation gate (`SkipRedundantShadowActivation`) and whatever residual cost the still-open sunny-map/content-dependent thread (see the user's own separate "we still have to chase the other regression which happens on certain maps or modes" note) accounts for. Traced `GetAsset`'s real call chain (`AssetInfoCollector::Visit_Dependency` -> `m_zone.m_pools.GetAsset` -> `GameGlobalAssetPools::GetAsset`, `src/ZoneCommon/Pool/GlobalAssetPool.cpp`) and found a real, generic robustness gap: `m_global_asset_pools[assetType]` is a raw `std::vector` index guarded only by `assert(assetType < m_global_asset_pools.size())` -- a **Release-build no-op** (this build is `/p:Configuration=Release`). ## 5. Motion blur was controller-only -- now reacts to real per-tick view-angle change from any input device

**Status: Superseded -- the universal-capture fix documented below regressed controller motion blur; see issue #2's newest round for the real root cause and the actual current (hybrid) fix, live-confirmed working for both input methods. This entry is kept as-written for its own real historical/technical content (the accumulator semantics explanation below is still accurate and useful) but the code snippet below no longer matches what's shipped.**

Direct user instruction: "also we should make motion blur not controller only(as that was always a limitation)."

**Root cause**: `g_motionBlurYawDeltaDegX64`/`g_motionBlurPitchDeltaDegX64` (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`, consumed by `RunPreOverlayMotionBlurPassIfEnabled` in `overlay_hud.cpp`) were only ever written from two places inside `Hook_MovementTick`: the controller-stick-input block and the gyro block. Real mouse/keyboard look happens entirely inside the native `g_realMovementTick` trampoline this hook calls through to -- a completely separate code path neither of those blocks ever touches -- so a keyboard/mouse player got zero motion blur regardless of how hard they looked around, purely because nothing ever fed the delta variables for that input class. The gating logic itself (`RunPreOverlayMotionBlurPassIfEnabled`) was NOT device-gated; the bug was entirely in how the blur *amount* got computed.

**Fix**: removed the per-source direct writes (both the active-branch/neutral-branch pair in the stick block, and the `+=` pair in the gyro block) and replaced them with a single universal before/after capture wrapped around the `g_realMovementTick(...)` call:

```cpp
const float preNativeYaw = g_yawAccum ? *g_yawAccum : 0.0f;
const float preNativePitch = g_pitchAccum ? *g_pitchAccum : 0.0f;

g_realMovementTick(param1, param2);

if (g_yawAccum) g_motionBlurYawDeltaDegX64 = preNativeYaw - *g_yawAccum;
if (g_pitchAccum) g_motionBlurPitchDeltaDegX64 = preNativePitch - *g_pitchAccum;
```

This relies on `g_yawAccum`/`g_pitchAccum`'s own already-documented real semantics (see that variable's header comment in the same file): controller/gyro write directly into these shared native accumulators BEFORE the native call; the native call itself ALSO adds real mouse/keyboard delta on top (accumulate, not overwrite -- controller and mouse correctly stack); then it packs the whole accumulated value into the real `usercmd_t` angle fields and writes back only a small leftover fractional remainder. So "value right before the native call" minus "value right after" equals the real TOTAL applied delta for that tick from every contributing input device at once, using the exact same sign convention the old per-source writes already used (every contributor here subtracts from the accumulator, so pre-minus-post comes out positive in the same direction the old `yawDelta`/`pitchDelta` values were).

The capture is placed unconditionally, before the K+M-safe-mode controller gate (`!g_modConfig.disableControllerInputX64`) -- so with `DisableControllerInputX64=1` (no controller/gyro contribution at all that tick), the capture still correctly isolates the real mouse-only delta, since the native call is the only remaining writer to the accumulator in that case.

Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, deployed). Not yet live-tested with a keyboard/mouse-only session. Commit `fa3ae124`.

## 6. `ForceAnisotropicFiltering`/`ForceHighQualityShadows`/`ForceHighQualityLighting` are silent no-ops on x64 (SP included, not just MP)

**Status: Open.** Found 2026-09-23 while scoping the visual-enhancement-suite port to `iw5mp.exe` (see the "MP visual-suite port scoping" round below) -- a genuinely new finding, not something the MP work introduced.

`x64_feature_parity_audit.md` rows #46-48 claimed all three of these were "PRESENT"/"confirmed firing on x64 via log evidence." That verdict is wrong, carried over uncritically from x86-era testing rather than re-verified on x64 -- the exact documentation-drift bug class this same audit file already caught itself doing once before (2026-09-13's own correction round).

**Real root cause**: `ApplyForcedAnisotropicFilteringIfEnabled`/`ApplyForcedHighQualityShadowsIfEnabled`/`ApplyForcedHighQualityLightingIfEnabled` (`overlay_hud.cpp`) have no arch guard themselves and unconditionally log `[aniso-force]`/`[shadow-quality-force]`/`[lighting-quality-force]` on every value change -- but each one's actual work happens through `SetDvarFloat`/`SetDvarBool` (`real_settings.cpp`), and those three setters (plus `SetDvarString`) were given an EXPLICIT, unconditional `#if defined(_M_X64) || defined(_WIN64)` early-return no-op on 2026-09-04, specifically to stop a crash from their own raw x86-only function pointers (`SetDvarBoolRaw`/`SetDvarFloatRaw`/`SetDvarStringRaw`, hardcoded addresses like `0x0044d700`/`0x005513c0`). The log line fires either way, since it lives in the caller, one layer above the silent no-op -- giving every appearance of a working feature while doing nothing at all on x64.

This is the SAME underlying gap `x64_feature_parity_audit.md` row #64 already documents in depth for the Custom Options screen's own vanilla-setting data layer (`GetDvarBool`/`Float`/`String` are dead on x64 the same way, `FindDvar()`'s `#ifdef _M_IX86`-only `__asm` always returns `nullptr`) -- these three forced-quality toggles are a second, independent set of callers hitting the exact same dead `real_settings.cpp` layer, just on the SETTER side rather than the getter side, and were missed by that row's own otherwise-thorough audit.

**Not the same code path as the already-working `FindDvarX64`/`GetDvarFloatX64`/`GetDvarStringX64`** (`analog_input_hooks_x64.cpp`, used by the ADS zoom-aware look-slowdown and Survival ready-up's mode gate) -- those are real, working x64 READS, resolved via signature scan per the locked policy, but no x64 WRITE equivalent has ever been built. Writing a dvar isn't just poking the same struct offset a getter reads (`GetDvarFloatX64` confirmed the float value lives at `dvarPtr+0x10`) -- the real engine setter almost certainly also handles min/max clamping, "latched" dvar semantics, and change-notification callbacks the way x86's own `SetDvarFloatRaw`/`SetDvarBoolRaw` do; a raw memory write to the value field would skip all of that, an unverified risk this project's own signature-scanning discipline ("fail loudly rather than hook/write garbage") argues against attempting without first confirming the real setter's actual behavior via decompile.

**Deliberately NOT fixed as part of the MP-porting work that surfaced it** -- this is a genuinely separate, deeper RE task (finding real x64 `SetDvarBool`/`SetDvarFloat`/`SetDvarString` native equivalents, the same missing piece row #64 already flagged blocks the Custom Options screen too) than "port an already-working SP feature to MP." Fixing it would benefit SP, MP, AND the already-deferred Custom Options screen data layer all at once, so it's worth doing as its own dedicated pass rather than folded into the MP visual-suite port. `InternalRenderScalePercent` (a pure D3D9-level render-target override, no dvar write involved at all) and `FsrSharpenEnabled`/motion blur (once their own MP-specific gate-signature work lands, see issue #4's sibling scoping notes) are unaffected by this bug and remain real, working candidates for the MP port.

**Second, independent, stronger motivation to prioritize this found the same day**: the renderer-architecture-mapping pass (`renderer_architecture_map.md` section 5b) turned up a complete, real, fully-named native SSAO feature -- `r_ssao`/`r_ssaoStrength`/`r_ssaoPower`/`r_ssaoBlurRadius`/`r_ssaoDownsample`/`r_ssaoDebug`, a real dvar set with full-res and downsampled quality tiers and its own debug visualization mode, never touched or even documented by this project before. Also directly relevant to `known_issues_x64.md` issue #2 (SMAA parked) -- `r_ssaoDebug` is a real, ready-to-use tool for testing whether native SSAO is involved in that pass's own "looks worse than off" symptom. Both this and the three forced-quality toggles above stay unforceable on x64 until this same underlying gap is closed -- fixing it once unlocks a substantially more valuable feature set than either use case alone.

## 9. Real, pre-existing game hang/freeze during extended play -- direct user report, first live-captured log evidence of a genuine deadlock, not a crash

**Status: Investigating.** Direct user report during issue #4's own live pause-vs-live testing (2026-09-26): "okay i went from repro, pause to healthy gameplay then before i paused on that the game froze and i force quit" -- followed by an explicit clarification once `GpuSyncTimingLogging` (issue #4's own new diagnostic tool, active for this capture) was flagged as a possible contributor: **"its contibuting but this has been existent throughout long before any of that stuff"** -- confirming this is a real, standing, pre-existing bug this project has not previously tracked, not something newly introduced by this session's own tooling. `GpuSyncTimingLogging` was disabled in the live config in response (`0`), but only as a contributing-factor mitigation, not treated as the root cause.

**Real, direct log evidence this is a genuine deadlock/hang, not a crash**: the session's `proxy_d3d9.log` ends with zero `proxy_d3d9 detach` lines anywhere -- confirming no clean DLL unload happened, consistent with a hard force-quit rather than a normal exit. The final 7 consecutive `[resource-diag]` samples (a dedicated background thread, logging real process/system memory once per second per this project's own event-driven threading architecture) show **completely static, byte-identical values** (`workingSetMB=3863.5 privateBytesMB=5774.3 pagefileUsageMB=5774.3`, unchanged across all 7 seconds) with zero disk I/O -- meaning the process was genuinely frozen, doing no real work, for at least 7 seconds before being killed, while at least one background thread kept ticking independently. This is the classic signature of a real deadlock (a thread blocked waiting on something that will never release) rather than a crash (which would show an exception/WER-adjacent log break, or the process simply vanishing rather than continuing to log static diagnostic lines).

**A real, secondary observation from the same capture, not yet connected to a cause**: `[x64-renderview-rate]`'s own frame counter stopped advancing at frame 1424 (its last logged entry: `frameMs=135.72 fps=7.4`, itself already a real slowdown from the prior ~12-20ms frames) and never produced another entry -- but `[x64-renderview-select-diag]` (a lower-level, per-view-activation-call diagnostic) kept firing for roughly 300 more calls afterward (~10 more full render-pass cycles at the observed ~27-28-call-per-pass rate), cycling through the same familiar view-index pattern (`13,2,1,10,5,2,14,12,6,13,2...`) with no further progress, before the log goes quiet entirely except for the background `[resource-diag]` heartbeat. This suggests the hang may not have been instantaneous -- the render/submission layer appears to have kept resubmitting similar work for a short while after the higher-level frame counter (likely tied to game-logic/simulation state) had already stopped advancing, before the whole process eventually locked up completely. Not yet root-caused; recorded here as a real, potentially load-bearing clue for whichever future session investigates this (a genuine simulation/logic-thread deadlock with the render thread spinning on stale state for a few seconds afterward would produce exactly this log shape).

**Real, honest scope note**: this is a first-report capture, not yet a reproduced-on-demand bug. The repro sequence (repro-mission gameplay -> pause -> unpause -> healthy-area gameplay -> attempting to pause again) is the only known context so far, and it's unclear yet whether any single step in that sequence is required, or whether this is a time/session-length-dependent hang that could occur during any sufficiently long play session regardless of the specific sequence. `GpuSyncTimingLogging` is now off by default in the live config as a precaution, but per the user's own direct statement this bug predates that tool entirely, so its removal should not be assumed to prevent a recurrence. **Real, concrete next step**: reproduce again with `GpuSyncTimingLogging=0` (now the live setting) to see if the hang still occurs: if it does, that's real, positive confirmation the tool wasn't the primary cause; if it doesn't recur across several further sessions, that would be circumstantial (not proof, given hangs are often intermittent) evidence worth investigating further despite the user's own recollection that this predates the tool.

**DECISIVE, same day, direct user test ("i did the slow map and pause first, then the fast map and paus[e]") -- pause adds a roughly FIXED absolute cost regardless of map, not a multiplicative one, cleanly explaining why every prior ratio (4x, 1.71x, 5.6x) looked real depending on which map was tested.** A single continuous session captured both maps and both pauses; segmented via the large state-transition hitches (level loads, pause open/close) bracketing each block:
- **Slow map gameplay** (immediately pre-pause): ~25ms/frame (~40fps).
- **Slow map pause** (frames 706-860, `renderViewFires=89`/`realTransitions=75`, a dense 155-sample plateau): **45.34ms/frame (~22.1fps)**.
- **Fast map gameplay** (frames 2400-3420, `renderViewFires=23`/`realTransitions=9`): **5.11ms/frame (~195.6fps average)**, with individual frames peaking at 280-394fps -- matching the user's own "gameplay spiked over 300" report exactly.
- **Fast map pause** (frames 3450-3570 + 3690-3750, same lower fires/transitions signature elevated well above baseline): **~26.8ms/frame (~37fps)**.

**The absolute added cost from pause is nearly identical on both maps**: slow map, 45.34 - 25 = **+20.3ms**; fast map, 26.8 - 5.11 = **+21.7ms** -- a striking match given how different the two maps' own baseline costs are. The RATIO differs wildly (slow map ~1.81x, fast map ~5.24x) purely because the same ~20-22ms fixed addition is being divided by a very different baseline -- on the already-expensive slow map it's a modest relative bump, on the genuinely cheap fast map it dominates. This is real, direct, decisive confirmation of the mechanism already traced via decompile (a fixed, roughly scene-light-count-independent extra cost from re-running the per-light shadow-dispatch loop a second time while paused) -- not a coincidence or measurement artifact. It also fully reconciles every previous, seemingly-inconsistent ratio this issue has produced: the original ~4x correlation, the ~1.71x same-repro-scene figure, and the ~5.6x true-healthy-gameplay figure were never actually in tension with each other -- they were all measuring the same ~20ms fixed adder against different baseline costs, and the "right" ratio to quote depends entirely on which map/scene is being compared against.

**Direct follow-up check, same test data, direct user instruction ("now look whats diff on the two maps") -- the slow map's own higher baseline cost is fully, proportionally explained by real per-light transition volume, NOT a separate x64-specific per-call cost anomaly.** Comparing `realTransitions` (the post-dedup, real-cost count -- not the raw `renderViewFires`, which is misleading here since it includes deduped no-ops) between the two maps' own gameplay segments: slow map 42 vs fast map 9 (**4.67x**), against a frametime ratio of 25ms/5.11ms (**4.89x**) -- these two ratios track almost exactly (~5% residual). This means the slow map is simply doing ~4.7x more real per-light/shadow-caster render-view work per frame (more active lights or shadow-casting geometry actually in view), and each unit of that work costs roughly the same either way -- a clean, expected, content-driven scaling relationship, not a new bug. **Useful negative result**: if this were the same disproportionate content regression already flagged elsewhere in this issue (sunny/bright maps running worse than their own light count would predict), the frametime ratio would be expected to exceed the transitions ratio by a real margin (extra, unexplained per-light cost beyond just doing more of the same real work) -- it doesn't here, they match closely. **CORRECTED, direct user pushback: "thats not how x86 worked tho for sure."** The "not a bug, just proportional content scaling" conclusion above only checked INTERNAL x64 consistency (does x64's own frametime track x64's own transition count) -- it never checked whether x86 ever showed anywhere near this size of gap BETWEEN these two specific maps in the first place, which is the real question for whether this is a regression. Direct user correction: x86 did not behave this way -- implying Dome and Underground ran at comparable framerates to each other on the original x86 build, nothing like x64's current ~4.67x real-transition-count / ~4.89x frametime spread between them. If that's accurate, the internal x64 consistency check above doesn't clear this pair at all -- it just means whatever inflated Dome's real per-light transition count so far above Underground's (relative to how these two maps compared on x86) is ITSELF the regression, even though x64's own downstream cost-per-transition scaling is behaving normally once that inflated count exists. **This reopens, rather than closes, the connection between this specific map pair and the still-open content-dependent regression thread** -- real next step, not yet done: find whether x86-era benchmark/performance data for these two specific Survival maps exists anywhere in this project's own history to confirm the magnitude of what x86 actually showed (rather than relying on recollection alone), and if so, RE why Dome's real per-light transition count is so much higher than Underground's specifically -- is it a genuinely higher light/shadow-caster count in that map's own content (which would still need explaining why x86 didn't show the same relative gap, e.g. a real per-light-type dvar/detection difference), or a real x64-side miscount/over-trigger specific to whatever Dome's content contains that Underground's doesn't.

**Map identification, direct user follow-up: "both survival maps here btw dome lags, underground fine."** Both maps tested this round are real Survival maps -- **Dome is the "slow map"** (42 `realTransitions`, ~25ms/~40fps gameplay baseline, the one that genuinely lags), **Underground is the "fast map"** (9 `realTransitions`, ~5ms/~195fps+ baseline, peaks 280-394fps, runs fine) -- Underground also matches this issue's own earlier session reference point ("Underground" was the map used for the original 160fps-live/40fps-paused live report that opened this whole investigation thread). Real, named ground truth for any future session revisiting this specific pair.

**Real second gap found and fixed same day, direct user follow-up ("yes but renderdoc too"): `InitRenderDocX64()` (issue #4's own RenderDoc F11 tool) had NO config gate at all -- it ran unconditionally on every single launch.** Checked directly: `dllmain.cpp`'s `Direct3DCreate9` forwarder called `InitRenderDocX64()` with zero `g_modConfig` check anywhere in the call path. Since RenderDoc has since been installed on this machine (`RenderDoc_1.46_64.msi`, downloaded this session for the F11 tool's own live-testing), `RENDERDOC_GetAPI()` now succeeds every launch and RenderDoc's own Vulkan capture layer attaches in-process for the WHOLE session regardless of whether F11 is ever pressed -- exactly the same class of "always-on third-party instrumentation sitting across every swapchain/device-state transition" concern as `GpuSyncTimingLogging`, just never previously gated at all (an oversight from when it was first built, since at that time RenderDoc wasn't yet installed and the code path was silently inert). **Fixed**: new `[Experimental] GpuCaptureEnabled` config key (default OFF), gating the `InitRenderDocX64()` call site directly in `dllmain.cpp` -- confirmed safe to gate on `g_modConfig` at that exact call site since `LoadModConfig()` runs unconditionally in `DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH`, always before the game can call the exported `Direct3DCreate9`. Build-verified (x64 Release, 0 errors, `dumpbin`-confirmed genuine x64 output), deployed. `GpuCaptureEnabled=0` documented in the live `mw3ncp_config.ini`. **Same honest caveat as `GpuSyncTimingLogging`**: this is a real, legitimate contributing-factor candidate for issue #9's hang, not a confirmed cause -- both diagnostic tools are now off by default, giving the cleanest possible baseline for reproducing (or failing to reproduce) issue #9 again without either one active.
